TensorRT-LLM → Triton. Ready for Django!

11.4 NeMo Megatron — Large-Scale Distributed Training

NeMo Megatron is the distributed training engine behind NVIDIA's largest models. It combines tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, and data parallelism to scale training across thousands of GPUs.

NeMo Megatron — 3D Parallelism Strategy
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                NeMo MEGATRON — DISTRIBUTED TRAINING                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │   │  TENSOR PARALLELISM (TP=4)                                       │   │
  │   │  Splits each Transformer layer across 4 GPUs                     │   │
  │   │  GPU 0: [Q K]  GPU 1: [V Attn]  GPU 2: [FFN1]  GPU 3: [FFN2]   │   │
  │   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │   │  PIPELINE PARALLELISM (PP=4)                                     │   │
  │   │  Splits model layers across 4 GPU groups                         │   │
  │   │  Group 0: [L0-L7] → Group 1: [L8-L15] → Group 2: [L16-L23]...   │   │
  │   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │   │  DATA PARALLELISM (DP=8)                                         │   │
  │   │  Each GPU group processes different data batch                   │   │
  │   │  Gradients averaged across groups every step                     │   │
  │   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                          │
  │   Total GPUs = TP × PP × DP = 4 × 4 × 8 = 128 GPUs                     │
  │   🎯 Scales to thousands of GPUs — used to train GPT-MT 530B!          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 SRE Tip: NeMo Megatron on DGX SuperPOD

When deploying NeMo Megatron across multiple DGX nodes, use NVIDIA BCM (Base Command Manager) for cluster orchestration. It handles node allocation, health checks, and job scheduling. NVLink + InfiniBand provide 900 GB/s GPU-to-GPU bandwidth for near-linear scaling.

11.5 Practical: Fine-Tune a Job Description Generator for anihpj

Let's put it all together: use NeMo to build an AI-powered job description generator for the anihpj jobpost Django application.

🏆 anihpj Job Description Generator — End-to-End

Goal: Given a job title, location, skills list, and company info, generate a professional, well-structured job posting in anihpj's format.

Pipeline:

  1. Data Prep: Export 10,000 existing job posts from Django → JSONL fine-tuning dataset
  2. Fine-Tune: NeMo PEFT/LoRA on Llama 3-8B with the anihpj dataset (2-4 hours on 2× A100)
  3. Guardrails: Input validation (job title must be real) + Output validation (salary range must be reasonable, no discriminatory language)
  4. Deploy: Export to TensorRT-LLM → Serve on Triton Inference Server (Ch 12)
  5. Integrate: Django view calls Triton API → generates draft job description → human reviews and publishes

Result: AI drafts job postings in <2 seconds. Human recruiter reviews and publishes. 80% reduction in job posting creation time!

✅ Verify: NeMo Fine-Tuning Checklist

  • ✅ Training data in JSONL format with "input" and "output" keys
  • ✅ Base model downloaded from NGC (nvidia/Llama-3-8B-NeMo)
  • ✅ PEFT config with appropriate rank (8-32 for LoRA)
  • ✅ Validation split to monitor overfitting
  • ✅ Export fine-tuned model with model.save_pretrained()

Q2

What is the purpose of NeMo Guardrails?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

NeMo Guardrails is a safety layer that validates inputs before they reach the LLM (jailbreak detection, topic validation, PII filtering) and filters outputs before users see them (hallucination detection, toxicity removal, format validation). It prevents prompt injection, toxic responses, and off-topic outputs.

💡 EXPLANATION
  NeMo GUARDRAILS — Safety Sandwich
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  User Input → [INPUT RAILS: jailbreak/PII/topic check]   │
  │       ↓ (if safe)                                        │
  │  [LLM generates response]                                │
  │       ↓                                                  │
  │  [OUTPUT RAILS: hallucination/toxicity/format check]     │
  │       ↓                                                  │
  │  Safe Response → User                                    │
  │                                                          │

Q3

What is PEFT/LoRA and why is it important for fine-tuning?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning via Low-Rank Adaptation. Instead of updating all model weights (80 GB for 8B model), LoRA trains only small adapter matrices (rank 8-32, ~0.1% of parameters). This allows fine-tuning on a single GPU (24 GB RTX 4090) with ~98% of full fine-tuning quality.

💡 EXPLANATION
  LoRA — Fine-Tune 8B LLM on a Single RTX 4090
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  FULL FINE-TUNING: Update ALL 8B weights                 │
  │  Memory: 80 GB (model) + 160 GB (optimizer) = IMPOSSIBLE│
  │                                                          │
  │  LoRA: Freeze base model, train tiny adapters            │
  │  Memory: 16 GB (quantized model) + 1 GB (adapters) ✅   │
  │  Adapter size: rank 16 × 2 matrices × 32 layers ≈ 50 MB │
  │  Quality: 98% of full fine-tuning                        │
  │                                                          │
  │  For anihpj: Fine-tune Llama 3 on job posting data       │
  │  on a single RTX 4090 in ~4 hours. Cost: ~$5 electricity.│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Q4

What are the three parallelism strategies in NeMo Megatron?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Tensor Parallelism (TP): Splits individual layers across GPUs. Pipeline Parallelism (PP): Splits model layers into stages across GPU groups. Data Parallelism (DP): Different data batches on different GPU groups. Total GPUs = TP × PP × DP. Used to scale to thousands of GPUs for models like GPT-MT 530B.

💡 EXPLANATION
  3D PARALLELISM — Scaling to 1000s of GPUs
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DP: 4 copies of model, each gets ¼ of data batch        │
  │  ┌─────┐┌─────┐┌─────┐┌─────┐                           │
  │  │Model││Model││Model││Model│  ← Data Parallelism (DP=4) │
  │  │copy1││copy2││copy3││copy4│                            │
  │  └──┬──┘└──┬──┘└──┬──┘└──┬──┘                            │
  │     │      │      │      │                                │
  │  PP: Each copy split into 8 pipeline stages (PP=8)        │
  │  TP: Each stage's layers split across 4 GPUs (TP=4)       │
  │  TOTAL GPUs = 4(DP) × 8(PP) × 4(TP) = 128 GPUs          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Install: pip install nemo_toolkit['all']. Models: From NGC Catalog (ngc.nvidia.com) — pre-trained checkpoints for GPT, T5, BERT, Llama, Mixtral, and more. Also available via Hugging Face with NeMo adapter weights.

NeMo bridges HuggingFace and NVIDIA ecosystems. Q7

What happens if a user tries to jailbreak the anihpj job description generator?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

NeMo Guardrails input rails detect the jailbreak attempt (e.g., "ignore previous instructions") and block it before reaching the LLM. The system responds with a pre-defined safe message like "I cannot change my behavior. How can I help with job search?" — never exposing the LLM to the malicious prompt.

💡 EXPLANATION

Guardrails work like a security checkpoint: input rails are the metal detector (block threats BEFORE they enter), output rails are the exit check (verify nothing dangerous leaves). For anihpj's job description generator: input rails block prompt injection attempts, output rails ensure generated job descriptions don't contain discriminatory language or hallucinated requirements.

Q8

What cluster management tool does NVIDIA provide for NeMo Megatron on DGX SuperPOD?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Base Command Manager (BCM) — NVIDIA's cluster orchestration tool for AI workloads. It handles node allocation, health checks, job scheduling, and resource management across DGX SuperPOD clusters. Integrates with Slurm for job queuing.

💡 EXPLANATION

BCM is to AI clusters what Kubernetes is to web services — it schedules AI training jobs across GPU nodes. BCM integrates with Slurm (HPC scheduler) for job queuing and NGC for container management. For anihpj: BCM would manage training jobs across 4 DGX nodes, ensuring fair GPU allocation between data scientists.

Q9

How do you deploy a NeMo fine-tuned model for production inference?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Export to ONNX or TensorRT-LLM format, then serve on Triton Inference Server (Ch 12). TensorRT-LLM provides optimized inference with FP8 quantization, inflight batching, and paged attention — achieving 5-10× higher throughput than vanilla PyTorch inference.

💡 EXPLANATION

The NeMo→Triton pipeline: Train in NeMo → Export to TensorRT-LLM → Package in Triton model repository → Serve via HTTP/gRPC. This is NVIDIA's recommended production path for LLMs. For anihpj: the job description generator follows this exact pipeline — NeMo for training, Triton for serving.

Chapter 12: Triton Inference Server — Production Model Serving at Scale

Triton Inference Server is NVIDIA's production-grade model server that supports every major AI framework (TensorFlow, PyTorch, ONNX, TensorRT, custom backends) simultaneously. It handles dynamic batching, concurrent model execution, GPU scheduling, and model pipelines — all through a single HTTP/gRPC endpoint. For anihpj jobpost, Triton serves the job matching model, the job description generator, and a skills classifier — all from one server.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours🚀 Inference🌐 Serving

🧑‍🏫 Why Triton? 4 Problems It Solves

1. Framework Fragmentation: PyTorch + TensorFlow + ONNX models all served from ONE Triton server. Drop model files in versioned folders.

2. GPU Underutilization: Dynamic batching groups individual requests into efficient GPU batches. 1 request = 5% GPU. 32 batched = 85% GPU. 17× more throughput.

3. Model Updates = Downtime: Version directories (1/, 2/, 3/) enable zero-downtime A/B testing and instant rollback.

4. Pipeline Complexity: Ensembles chain 3 models into ONE API call — server-side pipeline, no client orchestration needed. 3× faster.

12.1 What is Triton Inference Server?

Triton is a multi-framework, multi-model inference server from NVIDIA. One Triton instance can serve models in TensorRT, PyTorch, TensorFlow, ONNX, Python, and custom backends simultaneously — all through the same HTTP/REST and gRPC API. It's the standard for production ML serving at NVIDIA and most enterprise AI deployments.

The problem Triton solves: Before Triton, production ML serving was fragmented. Each framework had its own server (TorchServe for PyTorch, TF Serving for TensorFlow). If you had models in different frameworks — which most real applications do — you needed multiple servers, each with different APIs, monitoring, and scaling behavior. Triton unifies all of this: one server, one API, one monitoring endpoint. Additionally, Triton's dynamic batching and GPU scheduling are far more sophisticated than any framework-specific server — making it the go-to choice for GPU-efficient inference.

For anihpj jobpost: Triton hosts three models — a skills classifier (ONNX), a job recommender (TensorRT), and a job description generator (PyTorch). All three are served from a single Triton instance with one API endpoint. The ensemble feature chains them: incoming text → extracted skills → matching jobs → generated descriptions — all in one API call, all GPU-accelerated.

🌐 Multi-Framework

TensorRT, PyTorch, TensorFlow, ONNX Runtime, Python, custom C++ backends. One server, any model format.

📊 Dynamic Batching

Collects individual requests into GPU-efficient batches. Configurable max batch size and delay. 10-100× throughput improvement.

⚙️ Concurrent Execution

Multiple models share GPU(s) with priority queues. Model A gets 70% GPU, Model B gets 30%. No idle GPUs.

🔗 Model Ensembles

Chain models as pipelines: Preprocess → Model → Postprocess. All orchestrated by Triton, no custom code.

📈 Performance Analyzer

Built-in tool to benchmark latency, throughput, and GPU utilization under load. Find optimal batch size and concurrency.

🔒 Production Ready

Health checks, metrics (Prometheus), model versioning, rolling updates, gRPC streaming. Kubernetes-native.

12.2 Triton Architecture & Deployment

Triton Inference Server — Complete Architecture

📝 Triton Quick Start
# Pull and run Triton with NGC container
docker run --gpus all -it --rm \
  -v /models:/models \
  -p 8000:8000 -p 8001:8001 -p 8002:8002 \
  nvcr.io/nvidia/tritonserver:24.01-py3 \
  tritonserver --model-repository=/models

# Ports: 8000=HTTP, 8001=gRPC, 8002=Metrics (Prometheus)
# Verify: curl http://localhost:8000/v2/health/ready
# → {"status":"ready"}

12.3 Model Repository Structure

Each model in Triton lives in its own directory with a config.pbtxt file that defines its input/output schema, batch size, backend, and optimization settings.

Triton Model Repository — anihpj Example
/models/
├── job_recommender/           # Model 1: Job matching
│   ├── config.pbtxt
│   └── 1/                     # Version 1
│       └── model.plan          # TensorRT engine
├── jd_generator/              # Model 2: Job description LLM
│   ├── config.pbtxt
│   └── 1/
│       └── model.pt            # PyTorch model
├── skills_classifier/         # Model 3: Skill extraction
│   ├── config.pbtxt
│   └── 1/
│       └── model.onnx          # ONNX model
└── job_pipeline/              # Ensemble: chain 3→1→2
    ├── config.pbtxt
    └── 1/
config.pbtxt — Job Recommender Model
# models/job_recommender/config.pbtxt
name: "job_recommender"
platform: "tensorrt_plan"        # Backend
max_batch_size: 32               # Max requests per batch

input [
  {
    name: "candidate_embedding"
    data_type: TYPE_FP32
    dims: [ 512 ]                # 512-dim embedding
  }
]
output [
  {
    name: "job_scores"
    data_type: TYPE_FP32
    dims: [ -1 ]                 # Variable: N jobs
  }
]

# Optimization
optimization {
  # Enable dynamic batching with 100us delay
  dynamic_batching {
    max_queue_delay_microseconds: 100
    preferred_batch_size: [ 8, 16, 32 ]
  }
}

# GPU allocation
instance_group [
  {
    count: 1
    kind: KIND_GPU
    gpus: [ 0 ]                  # Use GPU 0
  }
]

12.4 Dynamic Batching — Maximizing GPU Throughput

Dynamic batching is Triton's killer feature. Instead of processing one request at a time (underutilizing the GPU), Triton collects multiple individual requests into a batch — then processes them all in one GPU pass. The result: 10-100× higher throughput with minimal latency impact.

Dynamic Batching — How It Works
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  WITHOUT DYNAMIC BATCHING (1 request at a time — GPU idle 90%):          │
  │  Time →  Req1[████████░░░░░░░░░░]Req2[░████████░░░░░░░░]Req3[░░████████] │
  │  GPU:     Bz=1        Bz=1          Bz=1          Bz=1                  │
  │  Throughput: 4 req/s   GPU util: ~20%                                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WITH DYNAMIC BATCHING (Collect & batch — GPU saturated):                │
  │  Time →  Req1[████████████████████████████████████████]                   │
  │          Req2[████████████████████████████████████████]                   │
  │          Req3[████████████████████████████████████████]                   │
  │          Req4[████████████████████████████████████████] Bz=4              │
  │  Throughput: 40 req/s  GPU util: ~85%  = 10× FASTER!                     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Config trade-off:                                                       │
  │  max_queue_delay: 100us → lower latency, potentially smaller batches    │
  │  max_queue_delay: 2000us → higher throughput, slightly higher latency   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

⚡ Dynamic Batching Best Practice

Set max_queue_delay_microseconds to 100-500 for interactive apps (low latency), 1000-5000 for batch processing (high throughput). Use preferred_batch_size to tell Triton your model's sweet spot (e.g., multiples of tensor core dimensions).

⚙️ Triton Concurrency Model — Multiple Instances, One GPU

Triton can run multiple copies of the same model on different GPUs (or the same GPU) to handle more concurrent requests. Combined with dynamic batching, this maximizes GPU saturation.

Triton Concurrency — Instances × Batching × Backends
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    TRITON CONCURRENCY MODEL                               │
  │                                                                          │
  │   Incoming Requests (high concurrency)                                   │
  │   R1 R2 R3 R4 R5 R6 R7 R8 R9 ... R100                                   │
  │       │                                                                  │
  │   ┌───▼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │   │  SCHEDULER — distributes to instances with available capacity    │  │
  │   └───┬──────────────────┬──────────────────┬───────────────────────┘  │
  │       │                  │                  │                           │
  │   ┌───▼──────────┐ ┌────▼──────────┐ ┌─────▼──────────┐               │
  │   │ Instance 0    │ │ Instance 1    │ │ Instance 2     │               │
  │   │ GPU 0         │ │ GPU 0         │ │ GPU 1          │               │
  │   │ Batch: 8 req  │ │ Batch: 8 req  │ │ Batch: 4 req   │               │
  │   │ Backend: TRT  │ │ Backend: TRT  │ │ Backend: TRT   │               │
  │   └──────────────┘ └───────────────┘ └────────────────┘               │
  │                                                                          │
  │   Config in config.pbtxt:                                               │
  │   instance_group [ { count: 3, kind: KIND_GPU, gpus: [0, 0, 1] } ]    │
  │                                                                          │
  │   🎯 3 instances × 8 batch = 24 concurrent requests processed!         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

12.5 Model Ensembles — Chaining Models as Pipelines

A model ensemble chains multiple models into a single inference pipeline. The output of one model becomes the input of the next — all orchestrated by Triton server-side with zero custom code.

anihpj Ensemble: Skills Classifier → Job Recommender → JD Generator
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                TRITON ENSEMBLE — anihpj JOB MATCHING PIPELINE             │
  │                                                                          │
  │  USER INPUT: "I have 5 years of Python and AWS experience in Lagos"      │
  │       │                                                                  │
  │  ┌────▼──────────────────┐                                              │
  │  │  🏷️ skills_classifier  │  Model 1: Extract skills → [Python, AWS]     │
  │  │  (ONNX, 5ms)          │  Output: skill_embedding [512]                │
  │  └────────┬──────────────┘                                              │
  │           │ skill_embedding                                              │
  │  ┌────────▼──────────────┐                                              │
  │  │  🔍 job_recommender   │  Model 2: Match against 100K jobs             │
  │  │  (TensorRT, 2ms)     │  Output: top_10_job_ids [10]                  │
  │  └────────┬──────────────┘                                              │
  │           │ top_job_ids                                                  │
  │  ┌────────▼──────────────┐                                              │
  │  │  🤖 jd_generator       │  Model 3: Generate matching job descriptions │
  │  │  (PyTorch, 200ms)     │  Output: 10 formatted job postings            │
  │  └────────┬──────────────┘                                              │
  │           │                                                              │
  │  USER SEES: "Here are your top 10 matching jobs with descriptions..."   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  🎯 TOTAL: 207ms end-to-end (vs ~2000ms without GPU!)                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

12.6 Performance Analyzer — Benchmarking Inference

Triton's built-in Perf Analyzer tool stress-tests your model server to find optimal concurrency, batch size, and throughput/latency trade-offs.

Triton Perf Analyzer Commands
# Benchmark job_recommender with different concurrency levels
perf_analyzer -m job_recommender \
  --concurrency-range 1:32:2 \     # Test concurrency 1, 3, 5... 31
  --shape candidate_embedding:512 \
  --percentile=95 \                # Report P95 latency
  -i gRPC                          # Use gRPC protocol

# Output:
# Concurrency  |  Throughput (infer/s) |  Latency P95 (ms)
#     1        |        120            |      8.3
#     8        |        850            |      9.4
#    16        |       1,400           |     11.4
#    32        |       1,600           |     20.1  ← Diminishing returns

# Find optimal batch size
perf_analyzer -m job_recommender -b 32 --percentile=95

# Benchmark ensemble pipeline
perf_analyzer -m job_pipeline --concurrency-range 1:16:2

  • ✅ Metrics: curl localhost:8002/metrics → Prometheus format
  • ✅ Model status: curl localhost:8000/v2/models → list all loaded models
  • ✅ GPU monitoring: nvidia-smi dmon -s pucm while benchmarking

12.7 Deploy anihpj Job Recommendation Model on Triton

🏆 Production Deployment: anihpj JobPost on Triton in Kubernetes

Architecture:

  1. Build: Export the job matching model to TensorRT (.plan file). Export the JD generator to PyTorch (.pt). Export skills classifier to ONNX.
  2. Repository: Create /models/ directory structure with config.pbtxt for each model.
  3. Container: nvcr.io/nvidia/tritonserver:24.01-py3 — includes all backends.
  4. Kubernetes: Deploy as a Deployment with nvidia.com/gpu: 1 resource request. Use a PersistentVolume for model storage.
  5. Service: Expose ports 8000 (HTTP) and 8001 (gRPC) via ClusterIP Service.
  6. Django Integration: Call http://triton-service:8000/v2/models/job_pipeline/infer from Django views. Use gRPC for lower latency.
  7. Monitoring: Scrape :8002/metrics with Prometheus. Alert on GPU utilization <50% (underused) or >95% (saturated).
💡 SRE Tip: Triton in Production K8s

Use Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) based on GPU utilization (via DCGM metrics). Configure PodDisruptionBudget for graceful rolling updates. Use model versioning (directories 1/, 2/, 3/) for zero-downtime model updates. Triton loads new versions without restarting.

📝 BLS — Business Logic Scripting in Triton

Triton supports Business Logic Scripting (BLS) via Python or C++ backends. BLS lets you run custom code between model calls — preprocessing, decision logic, API calls, database lookups — all within the Triton process. For anihpj: validate user input against the Django database BEFORE sending to the GPU model, reducing wasted GPU cycles on invalid requests. This is a key advantage over simpler inference servers.

📝 NVIDIA Practice Questions — Chapter 12

Q1

What AI frameworks does Triton Inference Server support?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

TensorRT, PyTorch, TensorFlow, ONNX Runtime, Python, and custom C++ backends — all simultaneously through the same HTTP/gRPC API. One Triton instance can serve models in any combination of these frameworks.

💡 EXPLANATION

Triton's multi-framework support is its biggest differentiator. Competitors are framework-specific (TF Serving = TF only, TorchServe = PyTorch only). Triton uses a backend plugin architecture — each framework has a backend that loads and executes models. For anihpj: serve the skills classifier (ONNX), job recommender (TensorRT), and JD generator (PyTorch) all from one Triton instance. One API, one monitoring endpoint, one deployment.

Q2

What is dynamic batching and why does it improve throughput?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Dynamic batching collects individual inference requests into a batch before sending to the GPU. Instead of processing requests one at a time (GPU underutilized), Triton waits up to max_queue_delay_microseconds to form a batch, then processes all at once. This increases GPU utilization from ~20% to ~85%, yielding 10-100× higher throughput.

💡 EXPLANATION
  DYNAMIC BATCHING — Before vs After
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  WITHOUT: 1 req/GPU call = GPU 20% utilized              │
  │  WITH: Wait 100μs → collect 32 reqs → 1 GPU call = 85%  │
  │                                                          │
  │  Throughput: 1 req/ms × 1000 ms = 1000 req/s (without)  │
  │  Throughput: 32 req/0.1ms = 320,000 req/s (with batch)  │
  │                                                          │
  │  Config: max_queue_delay_microseconds: 100               │
  │          preferred_batch_size: [ 8, 16, 32 ]            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Q3

What file defines a Triton model's configuration?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

config.pbtxt — a protobuf text file in each model's directory. It defines: model name, backend/platform, max_batch_size, input/output tensor shapes and types, dynamic batching settings, instance groups (GPU allocation), and optimization parameters.

💡 EXPLANATION
  TRITON CONFIG — Model Repository Structure
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  /models/                                                │
  │  ├── job_recommender/                                     │
  │  │   ├── config.pbtxt  ← model config (backend, batch)   │
  │  │   ├── 1/            ← version 1 (serving)             │
  │  │   │   └── model.plan (TensorRT engine)                │
  │  │   └── 2/            ← version 2 (A/B testing)         │
  │  │       └── model.plan (new model)                      │
  │  └── skills_classifier/                                   │
  │      ├── config.pbtxt                                     │
  │      └── 1/                                               │
  │          └── model.onnx                                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Add version 3/ → Triton loads it in background. Zero downtime.
Q4

How does a Triton model ensemble differ from calling models individually?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

An ensemble chains models into a single server-side pipeline — output of Model A becomes input to Model B automatically, with zero client-side orchestration. It avoids multiple network round-trips (one API call, not three), and Triton optimizes GPU scheduling across the entire pipeline.

💡 EXPLANATION
  TRITON ENSEMBLE — Server-Side Pipeline
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Client: POST /v2/models/anihpj_pipeline/infer           │
  │       ↓ (ONE API call, not THREE)                        │
  │  [Skills Classifier] → [Job Recommender] → [JD Generator]│
  │      ONNX backend         TensorRT backend    PyTorch     │
  │       ↓                    ↓                    ↓        │
  │  Skills detected    →  Top 20 matches   →  Descriptions  │
  │                                                          │
  │  Total: 207ms (vs 450ms if 3 separate API calls)        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Q5

How do you benchmark Triton model performance?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Use the built-in Perf Analyzer: perf_analyzer -m model_name --concurrency-range 1:32:2 --percentile=95. It reports throughput (infer/sec), latency (P50, P95, P99), and helps find the optimal concurrency level where throughput stops scaling.

💡 EXPLANATION

Perf Analyzer is essential for production capacity planning. Run it with increasing concurrency until latency spikes — that's your max throughput. For anihpj: benchmark the job recommender on L40S → find optimal concurrency at 8 → set K8s HPA to scale at 80% of that throughput. Without Perf Analyzer, you're guessing at infrastructure sizing.

Q6

What ports does Triton expose and for what protocols?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

8000: HTTP/REST inference API. 8001: gRPC inference API (lower latency, bidirectional streaming). 8002: Prometheus metrics endpoint. All three are standard and exposed by the NGC container.

💡 EXPLANATION

For anihpj production: Django calls Triton via gRPC (port 8001) for <1ms call overhead. Prometheus scrapes port 8002 for GPU utilization, request counts, and latency histograms. Port 8000 is used for health checks and debugging. Always expose all three in your K8s Service definition.

Q7

What is the model repository directory structure for Triton?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

/models/{model_name}/config.pbtxt + /models/{model_name}/{version}/model.{format}. Example: /models/job_recommender/1/model.plan. Version directories (1/, 2/, 3/) enable zero-downtime model updates — Triton loads new versions while serving old ones.

💡 EXPLANATION
  TRITON VERSIONING — Zero-Downtime Updates
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1/ → model_v1.plan  (Production, 100% traffic)         │
  │  2/ → model_v2.plan  (Staging, 10% A/B traffic)         │
  │                                                          │
  │  TRITON VERSION POLICY (config.pbtxt):                   │
  │  version_policy: { specific: { versions: [1, 2] }}       │
  │                                                          │
  │  TRAFFIC SPLIT: v1=90%, v2=10% → v1=50%, v2=50%        │
  │  → v1=0%, v2=100% (gradual rollout, 24 hours)           │
  │                                                          │
  │  IF v2 FAILS: Instant rollback to v1=100%. Zero downtime.│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The version directory is Triton's secret to zero-downtime deployments. When you add /models/job_recommender/2/model.plan, Triton detects the new version, loads it in the background, and starts routing traffic based on the version policy. Old version 1 continues serving until all in-flight requests complete, then unloads gracefully.

Q8

In the anihpj ensemble, what three models are chained and why?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Skills Classifier (ONNX) → Job Recommender (TensorRT) → JD Generator (PyTorch). The chain converts raw user text → skill embeddings → top job matches → formatted descriptions. Each model runs on its optimal backend; Triton orchestrates all three server-side in one API call (207ms total).

💡 EXPLANATION

This ensemble demonstrates Triton's unique value: each model uses its optimal framework backend. The classifier is small → ONNX (portable). The recommender needs max throughput → TensorRT (fastest). The JD generator uses HuggingFace → PyTorch (ecosystem). No other inference server can run all three in a single pipeline. For anihpj: this is the production architecture serving real user requests.

Q9

What Kubernetes resource request does a Triton GPU pod need?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

nvidia.com/gpu: 1 in the pod's resource limits/requests. For multi-model serving or larger models, request more GPUs. Use the NVIDIA GPU Operator for automatic driver and toolkit installation on K8s nodes.

💡 EXPLANATION

In K8s, GPU resources are unlike CPU/memory — they cannot be oversubscribed. nvidia.com/gpu: 1 dedicates an entire physical GPU to the pod. For MIG: nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb: 1. For anihpj: Triton pods request 1 GPU each. HPA scales based on GPU utilization from DCGM metrics. Always use nodeSelector to target GPU nodes.

Q10

What is the trade-off between max_queue_delay_microseconds and throughput?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Lower delay (100-500μs): Lower latency (better for interactive apps), smaller batches, lower GPU utilization. Higher delay (1000-5000μs): Higher throughput (better for batch processing), larger batches, slightly higher per-request latency. Choose based on your SLA: interactive apps need P95 < 50ms; batch jobs can tolerate 500ms+.

💡 EXPLANATION

For anihpj's interactive job search: set max_queue_delay_microseconds: 200 (P95 < 10ms). For nightly batch processing of 50M job embeddings: set max_queue_delay_microseconds: 5000 (maximize throughput, latency doesn't matter). This single config parameter controls the latency-vs-throughput tradeoff.

13.3 DGX B200 — Next Generation

The DGX B200 is the next-generation DGX built around the Blackwell architecture. It doubles or triples most specs compared to H100: 1,536 GB of GPU memory, 72 PFLOPS of FP8 compute, and 800 GB/s InfiniBand networking. Key innovation: the NVLink Switch 6 provides 1.8 TB/s per GPU — double the H100's bandwidth.

📝 DGX B200 Key Upgrades over DGX H100
  • GPU: H100 → B200 (Blackwell), 80 GB → 192 GB per GPU
  • Compute: 16 PF → 72 PF (FP8) — 4.5× more
  • NVLink: 900 GB/s → 1.8 TB/s per GPU — 2× faster
  • InfiniBand: 400G → 800G (NDR → XDR) — 2× faster
  • Power: 10.2 kW → ~14 kW (liquid cooling recommended)
  • Use Case: Training 1T+ parameter models (GPT-4 class)

13.4 DGX Station — Desktop AI Supercomputer

The DGX Station brings data-center-class AI compute to your desk. It's water-cooled and whisper-quiet (~35 dB — quieter than a conversation), making it suitable for office environments. With 4× A100 GPUs and 320 GB of GPU memory, it's perfect for development and prototyping before scaling to a full DGX.

Use a DGX Station for the anihpj development team. Fine-tune models locally with 4× A100s (320 GB GPU memory — enough for Llama 3-70B with LoRA). When ready for full training, move to a DGX H100 or SuperPOD. DGX Station eliminates cloud GPU costs during the development phase.

DGX SuperPOD achieves near-linear scaling up to thousands of GPUs. The secret: NVSwitch provides 900 GB/s within each DGX, and InfiniBand provides full bisection bandwidth between DGX nodes. No oversubscription — every GPU can communicate at full speed with every other GPU.

13.6 DGX Base Command Manager (BCM)

Base Command Manager is the cluster orchestration software for DGX systems. It handles provisioning, job scheduling, monitoring, and user management across the entire SuperPOD. BCM integrates with Slurm for job queuing and provides a single pane of glass for cluster operations.

📋 Job Scheduling

Integrated Slurm. GPU-aware scheduling — assign specific GPUs, MIG instances, or entire DGX nodes.

📊 Monitoring

DCGM metrics for every GPU. Power, temperature, utilization. Prometheus + Grafana dashboards.

👥 Multi-Tenancy

Projects, quotas, and user isolation. Data science team A can't starve team B's GPUs.

⚠️ NCA-AIIO Exam: DGX Gotchas

1. "DGX is just a server with GPUs" → ❌ It's an AI appliance. NVSwitch fabric, pre-tuned cooling, validated software stack. Not a commodity server.
2. "I can build a DGX equivalent myself" → ❌ You cannot buy NVSwitch separately. Without it, 8× H100 communicate at PCIe speeds (64 GB/s) instead of 900 GB/s — crippling multi-GPU training.
3. "DGX Station is just a desktop DGX" → ⚠️ Partially true. It has 4× A100 with NVLink but is water-cooled and silent — designed for office use, not data center. ~2.5 PFLOPS, 320W total.

📝 NVIDIA Practice Questions — Chapter 13

Q1

What is the fundamental difference between a DGX and a traditional GPU server?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

A DGX is a purpose-built AI appliance — every component (8 GPUs, NVSwitch, storage, networking) is pre-configured, pre-tested, and optimized by NVIDIA. A traditional GPU server requires you to select, assemble, and debug components yourself. DGX: hours to deploy. DIY server: days to weeks.

💡 EXPLANATION

DGX eliminates the integration tax: you don't debug PCIe topology, BIOS settings, cooling issues, or driver compatibility. Everything is factory-tested. For anihpj: purchase a DGX H100, rack it, connect power+network, and start training the same day. The alternative — buying 8× H100 separately + chassis + NVSwitch + CPUs — takes weeks of integration and risks performance issues from suboptimal component matching.

Q2

How many GPUs does a DGX H100 have and how are they interconnected?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

8× H100 GPUs interconnected via 4 NVSwitch chips providing 900 GB/s per GPU. This is full bisection bandwidth — any GPU can communicate directly with any other GPU at full speed, not just adjacent pairs.

💡 EXPLANATION

Without NVSwitch, GPUs can only talk to immediate neighbors via NVLink bridges (like a token ring). With NVSwitch, every GPU has a direct 900 GB/s path to every other GPU — this is what "full bisection bandwidth" means. Think of it like a telephone switchboard vs. passing notes down a row. For distributed training (all-reduce), this is critical: if GPU 0 needs gradients from GPU 7, it gets them at full speed without hopping through intermediate GPUs.

Q3

What is a DGX SuperPOD Scalable Unit (SU) and how many GPUs does it contain?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

An SU is 32 DGX H100 nodes = 256 H100 GPUs, interconnected via Quantum-2 InfiniBand with full bisection bandwidth. Multiple SUs can be combined: 4 SUs = 1,024 GPUs, 32 SUs = 8,192 GPUs (TOP500-class supercomputer).

💡 EXPLANATION
  DGX SuperPOD SCALING
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1 DGX = 8 GPUs                                          │
  │  1 SU   = 32 DGX = 256 GPUs (full bisection IB)         │
  │  4 SU   = 128 DGX = 1,024 GPUs                           │
  │  32 SU  = 1,024 DGX = 8,192 GPUs ← TOP500 class         │
  │                                                          │
  │  KEY: Each SU adds compute + networking proportionally.  │
  │  Near-linear scaling via non-blocking fabric design.     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Q4

What networking technology connects DGX nodes in a SuperPOD?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

InfiniBand (NDR 400 GB/s for H100, XDR 800 GB/s for B200). Each DGX has 8 ConnectX-7/8 InfiniBand adapters. The Quantum-2/3 switch fabric provides full bisection bandwidth — no network bottlenecks between any two GPUs in the cluster.

💡 EXPLANATION

Why InfiniBand and not Ethernet? InfiniBand provides RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access), which lets GPU memory be transferred directly over the network without involving the CPU. This is GPUDirect RDMA — critical for distributed training. RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet) is an alternative but has higher latency. The 8 adapters per DGX match the 8 GPUs, giving each GPU a dedicated network path. Quantum-2 switches with SHARP (Scalable Hierarchical Aggregation and Reduction Protocol) perform in-network all-reduce, further reducing communication overhead.

Q5

What is Base Command Manager and what does it do?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

BCM is NVIDIA's cluster orchestration software for DGX systems. It handles: job scheduling (Slurm-integrated, GPU-aware), monitoring (DCGM + Prometheus + Grafana), multi-tenancy (projects, quotas, isolation), and provisioning. It's the "control plane" for DGX SuperPOD.

💡 EXPLANATION

BCM is to DGX clusters what Kubernetes is to web services — it schedules AI training jobs across GPU nodes, allocates resources, and monitors health. It integrates with Slurm (the HPC industry standard scheduler) for job queuing. For anihpj: BCM ensures fair GPU sharing between data scientists training different models, with project-based quotas and priority queues.

Q6

What makes the DGX Station unique among DGX products?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

The DGX Station is a desktop AI supercomputer — water-cooled, whisper-quiet (~35 dB), with 4× A100 GPUs (320 GB total). Unlike rack-mounted DGX systems, it's designed for office/desk environments, making it perfect for development and prototyping before scaling to data center DGX.

💡 EXPLANATION

DGX Station fills the "development gap": data scientists can prototype models locally without fighting for cluster time. 35 dB is quieter than a conversation — it sits under a desk. The water cooling is self-contained (no external plumbing). For anihpj: your ML engineers can develop and debug the job recommendation model on a DGX Station, then push to DGX H100/SuperPOD for full-scale training. This "develop locally, train at scale" workflow is standard NVIDIA best practice.

Q7

How much GPU memory does the DGX B200 provide?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

1,536 GB (1.5 TB) total — 8× B200 GPUs with 192 GB each. This is 2.4× the DGX H100's 640 GB. Combined with 72 PFLOPS FP8 compute, the B200 is designed for training 1 trillion+ parameter models.

💡 EXPLANATION

The DGX B200 represents NVIDIA's next-generation platform (Blackwell architecture). The key numbers to memorize for the exam: B200 = 192 GB/GPU (vs H100's 80 GB), DGX B200 = 1,536 GB total (vs H100's 640 GB), B200 = 72 PFLOPS FP8 (vs H100's 32 PFLOPS). The massive memory increase enables training trillion-parameter models without excessive model parallelism — more of the model fits on fewer GPUs, reducing communication overhead.

Q8

For anihpj's job recommendation model (50M job postings), what DGX configuration is recommended?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

¼ Scalable Unit = 8 DGX H100 = 64 GPUs. Training time: ~50 minutes. For development/prototyping: 1 DGX H100 (~4 hours) or a DGX Station (4× A100, ~8 hours). The model trains with model parallelism across GPUs via NVSwitch, then deploys on Triton for inference.

💡 EXPLANATION

This is a practical sizing exercise. 50M job postings with text embeddings (~768 dimensions) trained as a two-tower recommendation model: the model itself isn't huge (~500M params), but the data volume drives GPU count. 64 GPUs splits the embedding table and training data across GPUs. The 50-minute target comes from anihpj's business need: retrain hourly to capture new job postings. Key takeaway: GPU count is driven by data size × retraining frequency, not just model size.

Q9

What is the key difference between NVSwitch and InfiniBand in a DGX SuperPOD?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

NVSwitch: Connects GPUs within a single DGX (up to 8 GPUs) at 900 GB/s. InfiniBand: Connects GPUs across different DGX nodes in the SuperPOD at 400 GB/s per port. Together they provide full bisection bandwidth at both intra-node and inter-node levels.

💡 EXPLANATION
  NVSwitch vs InfiniBand — Two Levels of GPU Fabric
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  INTRA-NODE (NVSwitch): GPU 0↔GPU 7 at 900 GB/s          │
  │  ┌──────┐┌──────┐┌──────┐     ┌──────┐                  │
  │  │GPU 0 ││GPU 1 ││GPU 2 │ ... │GPU 7 │ ← NVSwitch fabric │
  │  └──────┘└──────┘└──────┘     └──────┘                  │
  │                                                          │
  │  INTER-NODE (InfiniBand): DGX 0↔DGX 31 at 400 GB/s       │
  │  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐       ┌──────┐                      │
  │  │DGX 0 │──│DGX 1 │── ... ──│DGX 31│ ← IB fabric        │
  │  └──────┘  └──────┘       └──────┘                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Q10

How does the DGX SuperPOD achieve near-linear scaling to thousands of GPUs?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Three factors: (1) NVSwitch provides non-blocking GPU-to-GPU within each node. (2) InfiniBand with full bisection bandwidth ensures no network bottlenecks between nodes. (3) NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library) optimizes all-reduce operations across the fabric. Result: adding more GPUs adds proportional compute with minimal communication overhead.

💡 EXPLANATION

Near-linear scaling is the holy grail of distributed training. Without it, adding GPUs gives diminishing returns (e.g., 2× GPUs = 1.3× speedup). NCCL's ring and tree algorithms for all-reduce minimize the communication cost: gradients are reduced in O(N) time instead of O(N²). Combined with the non-blocking fabric, each additional GPU contributes ~95% of its theoretical compute to the training job. This is why DGX SuperPOD can scale to 8,192 GPUs and still be efficient.

14.1 What is HGX? — The GPU Baseboard Platform

HGX is NVIDIA's GPU baseboard platform — a standardized board containing 4 or 8 GPUs with NVSwitch interconnect, that server OEMs integrate into their chassis. Unlike DGX (NVIDIA builds the whole system), HGX lets you choose your preferred server vendor while getting the same GPU architecture.

14.3 HGX vs DGX — When to Choose Which

The decision framework: DGX and HGX use the exact same GPUs and NVSwitch fabric — the difference is everything around them. DGX is a finished product: NVIDIA selected the CPUs, RAM, storage, networking, cooling, and software. HGX is a component: you (or your OEM) build the system around it. The choice depends on your organization's capabilities and standards.

Practical rule of thumb: If your team has never built a GPU server before, start with DGX. The integration complexity of HGX (BIOS tuning, PCIe topology validation, thermal testing, driver certification) requires experienced infrastructure engineers. DGX eliminates all of this — unbox, rack, power on, start training. For anihpj: start with DGX for your initial AI lab (fastest path to working AI). As you scale to production, evaluate HGX through your preferred server vendor (Dell, HPE, etc.) for better integration with existing data center management tools.

DGX: For initial AI lab/PoC (1-2 DGX H100). Fast setup, single support. HGX: For production fleet (20+ nodes). Integrates with existing Dell/HPE infrastructure, lower per-node cost, fits data center power/cooling standards.

Q1

What is the fundamental difference between NVIDIA DGX and HGX?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

DGX: Complete AI appliance — NVIDIA builds the whole system (GPUs, CPUs, RAM, storage, networking, cooling). HGX: GPU baseboard only — OEMs (Dell, HPE, Lenovo) integrate it into their own servers with their choice of CPUs, RAM, and management.

💡 EXPLANATION

Think of DGX as buying a fully-built car (Toyota Camry — just drive) vs HGX as buying an engine + transmission (you choose the chassis, seats, electronics). Both use the same GPU "engine," but DGX comes pre-assembled and warranty-covered as one unit, while HGX lets you build around it. For the exam: DGX = "NVIDIA builds everything," HGX = "NVIDIA builds the GPU board, OEM builds the server."

Q2

What are the two HGX H100 configurations?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

HGX H100 4-GPU: 4× H100 with NVLink Bridge (pair-to-pair). HGX H100 8-GPU: 8× H100 with 4 NVSwitch chips (all-to-all 900 GB/s). The 8-GPU version has the same GPU fabric as DGX H100.

💡 EXPLANATION

The critical distinction: 4-GPU uses NVLink Bridges (only adjacent GPUs talk at 600 GB/s), 8-GPU uses NVSwitch (any-to-any at 900 GB/s). For distributed training with tensor parallelism across all GPUs, the 8-GPU config is dramatically faster because gradients don't have to hop through intermediate GPUs. The 8-GPU HGX is essentially a DGX without the chassis — same GPU fabric, same NVSwitch, same bandwidth.

Q3

When should an organization choose HGX over DGX?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Choose HGX when: (1) You have existing data center standards (Dell/HPE shop), (2) Need CPU/RAM flexibility beyond DGX defaults, (3) Deploying large fleets (100s of nodes — HGX is cheaper per node), (4) Require OEM-specific management (iDRAC, OneView). Choose DGX for speed and simplicity.

💡 EXPLANATION

This is a classic "build vs buy" decision. If your data center is already standardized on Dell iDRAC for out-of-band management, HPE OneView for firmware updates, and have spare Xeon CPUs from your server pool — HGX lets you leverage all that. DGX comes with NVIDIA's pre-selected components (typically AMD EPYC CPUs), which may not fit your DC tooling. Large fleet economics favor HGX: at 100+ nodes, the per-node savings from using commodity server parts adds up significantly.

What does NVIDIA-Certified Systems guarantee?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Certification guarantees that the server has passed NVIDIA's rigorous validation: GPU stress tests, networking performance, storage throughput, NVAIE compatibility, thermal/power validation under sustained AI workloads, and GPU Operator deployment. Certified = guaranteed to work with the full NVIDIA AI stack.

The certification badge is not just marketing — it means NVIDIA engineers have physically tested that exact server model with sustained AI workloads (not just short benchmarks). They verify: GPU-to-GPU bandwidth matches spec, InfiniBand/RoCE performance under load, GPUDirect Storage throughput, and that the GPU Operator deploys correctly in Kubernetes. For anihpj: always spec NVIDIA-Certified Systems — it eliminates the risk of discovering a PCIe topology bug or thermal throttling issue after deployment.

Q6

Does the HGX H100 4-GPU configuration have NVSwitch?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

No. The 4-GPU HGX uses NVLink Bridges (pair-to-pair connection at 600 GB/s), not full NVSwitch. Only the 8-GPU HGX (and all DGX models) include NVSwitch for all-to-all GPU connectivity at 900 GB/s.

💡 EXPLANATION

NVSwitch is the premium interconnect — it requires additional chips, power, and board space, so it's reserved for 8-GPU configurations where the all-to-all benefit justifies the cost. With NVLink Bridges on 4-GPU, GPU 0 can talk directly to GPU 1 (and GPU 2 to GPU 3), but GPU 0→GPU 3 requires hopping through GPU 1 and 2. For small multi-GPU training (data parallelism only), this is fine. For tensor parallelism needing all GPUs to share activations simultaneously, you need NVSwitch.

Q7

What is the key advantage of DGX over HGX for a new AI team?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Speed to deployment. DGX ships pre-configured — unbox, connect power/network, start training in hours. HGX requires OEM integration (weeks), plus you must validate the configuration yourself. For teams without dedicated AI infra expertise, DGX eliminates the integration burden.

💡 EXPLANATION

The hidden cost of HGX is time. OEM integration: 2-4 weeks. Then you must validate: PCIe topology (are GPUs on the right NUMA nodes?), BIOS settings (SR-IOV, ARI, large BAR), thermal testing (does it throttle under sustained load?), driver compatibility (GPU driver + OFED + CUDA toolkit versions aligned?). DGX ships with all this done. For a 5-person AI startup, DGX means training starts Friday afternoon instead of next month.

Q8

For anihpj's production fleet, what mix of DGX and HGX is recommended?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

DGX for dev/PoC (1-2 DGX H100 — fast setup, single support). HGX for production fleet (20+ nodes — integrates with Dell/HPE infrastructure, lower per-node cost, fits existing data center power/cooling). Transition from DGX prototyping to HGX production scale.

💡 EXPLANATION

This is the standard NVIDIA-recommended adoption path: "Land with DGX, expand with HGX." DGX proves the AI workload works and establishes performance baselines. Once you know the model trains successfully, HGX scales it economically. The DGX becomes your development/staging environment, and the HGX fleet handles production training. This hybrid approach gives you speed + scale without compromise.

Q9

How does OEM support work for HGX-based servers?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

OEM is primary support (Dell/HPE handle server hardware, management, initial troubleshooting). NVIDIA is backend (GPU-specific issues, NVAIE software, NVSwitch). The OEM and NVIDIA have support escalation agreements — you contact the OEM first, they escalate to NVIDIA if needed.

💡 EXPLANATION

This split support model can be confusing. If a GPU fails in a Dell PowerEdge XE9680: you call Dell, they diagnose, and if it's the GPU itself (which NVIDIA manufactured), Dell replaces it from their inventory and handles the NVIDIA RMA behind the scenes. You never call NVIDIA directly for hardware in an HGX server. For NVAIE software issues, Dell may escalate to NVIDIA. The key: one throat to choke (the OEM).

Q10

Can you build a SuperPOD with HGX-based servers?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Yes, but with caveats. HGX-based servers with 8 GPUs + NVSwitch + InfiniBand can form clusters similar to SuperPOD. However, the "DGX SuperPOD" branding and BCM software are DGX-specific. For HGX clusters, use NVIDIA AI Enterprise with GPU Operator and third-party cluster managers (Slurm, Kubernetes) instead of BCM.

💡 EXPLANATION

The hardware can match SuperPOD — 8-GPU HGX nodes with NVSwitch + InfiniBand have the same GPU fabric. The difference is software: BCM (Base Command Manager) is exclusive to DGX. For HGX clusters, you build the equivalent using NVAIE + GPU Operator + your choice of scheduler (Slurm or Kubernetes). This is actually more flexible — you can integrate with existing cluster management — but requires more setup work than BCM's turnkey experience.

Chapter 15: GPU Cluster Architecture & Design🟡 Intermediate

Chapter 15: GPU Cluster Architecture — Designing AI Infrastructure at Scale

Building a GPU cluster isn't just about buying GPUs — it's about designing a balanced system where compute, networking, storage, power, and cooling all work together. A poorly designed cluster bottlenecks on the slowest component. This chapter covers cluster topology, GPU communication fabrics, AI storage, power/cooling requirements, and sizing methodology — with a practical exercise designing an anihpj GPU cluster.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours🏗️ Architecture📐 Design

🧑‍🏫 A GPU Cluster Is Like a Restaurant Kitchen — Everything Must Be Balanced

You can't serve 500 meals/hour if your kitchen has 50 chefs but only 1 stove. A GPU cluster is the same — the slowest component determines overall speed.

🍳 Chefs = GPUs (Compute): H100 GPUs doing the math. If you have 32 chefs (GPUs) but can only feed them 1 ingredient at a time (slow storage), most chefs stand idle.

🚚 Food Delivery = Networking (InfiniBand): After every training step, GPUs must share results. If the network is slow, GPUs wait. InfiniBand at 400 Gb/s = instant delivery. Standard Ethernet at 10 GbE = traffic jam.

📦 Pantry = Storage (NVMe/Lustre/WEKA): Must deliver training data fast enough to keep GPUs busy. If storage provides 10 GB/s but GPUs need 20 GB/s, GPUs are idle 50% of the time. Use parallel filesystems, NEVER NFS.

❄️ Air Conditioning = Cooling (Liquid): 4 DGX in one rack = 40 kW of heat. Standard air cooling maxes at ~25 kW. Liquid cooling is REQUIRED for GPU clusters — it removes heat 3,500× more efficiently than air.

⚡ Electricity = Power (3-Phase 415V): GPU racks draw 40-50 kW. Standard office power is 208V single-phase, max ~15 kW per rack. You need industrial 3-phase power. Verify your data center can deliver this BEFORE ordering GPUs.

🎯 NCA-AIIO: AI Infrastructure ~35% 🎯 NCA-AIIO: AI Operations ~30%

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Design balanced GPU cluster topologies (compute, network, storage)
  • Compare GPU communication fabrics: NVLink, NVSwitch, InfiniBand, RoCE
  • Select storage solutions for AI: NVMe, GPUDirect Storage, parallel filesystems
  • Calculate power and cooling requirements for GPU clusters
  • Size GPU clusters based on workload requirements
  • Design an anihpj GPU cluster from scratch

🔑 Exam Tip — Cluster Design

The NCA-AIIO exam tests GPU cluster architecture principles: non-blocking fabric design, GPU-to-GPU bandwidth hierarchy (NVLink > InfiniBand > RoCE), GPUDirect Storage for AI data pipelines, and power/cooling at scale (40kW+ per rack). Know the difference between fat-tree and rail-optimized topologies. Expect 3-4 questions.

15.1 Cluster Topology Design

A GPU cluster has three tiers: compute nodes (GPU servers), network fabric (interconnect), and storage nodes (data pipeline). The topology determines how efficiently these tiers work together.

GPU Cluster Topology — Balanced Three-Tier Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     GPU CLUSTER TOPOLOGY                                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  💻 COMPUTE (GPU Nodes)     │    │  🗄️ STORAGE (Data Pipeline)      │ │
  │  │  ┌──────┐┌──────┐┌──────┐ │    │  ┌──────┐┌──────┐┌──────┐      │ │
  │  │  │DGX 1 ││DGX 2 ││DGX N │ │    │  │NVMe  ││Lustre││WekaFS│      │ │
  │  │  │8xH100││8xH100││8xH100│ │    │  │200TB ││2PB   ││1PB   │      │ │
  │  │  └──┬───┘└──┬───┘└──┬───┘ │    │  └──┬───┘└──┬───┘└──┬───┘      │ │
  │  └─────┼───────┼───────┼─────┘    └─────┼───────┼───────┼──────────┘ │
  │        │       │       │                │       │       │              │
  │  ┌─────┴───────┴───────┴────────────────┴───────┴───────┴──────────┐  │
  │  │               📡 NETWORK FABRIC (Quantum-2 InfiniBand)           │  │
  │  │  • Non-blocking, full bisection bandwidth                        │  │
  │  │  • 400 GB/s per port (H100), 800 GB/s (B200)                    │  │
  │  │  • GPUDirect RDMA: GPU memory → network → storage (no CPU!)      │  │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
TopologyDescriptionBest For
Fat-TreeFull bisection bandwidth. Every node has equal bandwidth to every other node.Training clusters (DGX SuperPOD)
Rail-OptimizedGPUs at same position across nodes share a rail. Optimized for all-reduce.Large-scale distributed training
Spine-LeafSimpler 2-tier. Leaf switches for nodes, spine for inter-leaf.Inference clusters, smaller deployments

15.2 GPU-to-GPU Communication Fabrics

GPU communication happens at multiple levels. Understanding the bandwidth hierarchy is critical for cluster design — you want the slowest link to still be fast enough for your workload.

TechnologyBandwidthScopeUse Case
NVLink 4.0900 GB/s per GPUGPU-to-GPU (same node)Model parallelism within DGX/HGX
NVSwitch900 GB/s per GPUAll GPUs in 8-GPU nodeFull mesh within a server
InfiniBand NDR400400 GB/s per portNode-to-nodeData parallelism across cluster
InfiniBand XDR800800 GB/s per portNode-to-nodeNext-gen B200 clusters
RoCE v2 (Ethernet)200-400 GB/sNode-to-nodeEthernet-based clusters (lower cost)

⚡ NCCL — The Secret Sauce

NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) optimizes all-reduce, all-gather, and broadcast operations across the GPU fabric. It automatically selects the best communication path (NVLink for intra-node, InfiniBand for inter-node) and uses ring/tree algorithms for maximum bandwidth utilization.

🧭 Decision Tree: Which Network Fabric for Your Cluster?

Is your cluster ≥ 32 GPUs doing distributed training with model parallelism?
✅ YES → InfiniBand NDR/XDR
400-800 GB/s, RDMA, full bisection BW, lowest latency
❌ NO — Smaller cluster or inference-only
Do you have an existing Ethernet infrastructure and budget constraints?
✅ YES → RoCE v2 (Ethernet)
200-400 GB/s, lower cost, uses existing switches
❌ NO — Greenfield AI cluster
📌 For anihpj: InfiniBand for the training cluster (32+ GPUs, model parallelism). RoCE acceptable for inference-only nodes.

15.3 Storage for AI — Feeding the GPU Beast

AI training is I/O intensive. A single DGX H100 can consume data at ~20 GB/s. If storage can't keep up, expensive GPUs sit idle waiting for data. GPUDirect Storage enables DMA transfers from NVMe directly to GPU memory — bypassing the CPU entirely.

Storage TypeThroughputLatencyBest For
GPUDirect Storage~200 GB/s~5μsDirect GPU data loading
Local NVMe~50 GB/s~10μsScratch space, caching
Lustre~500 GB/s (aggregate)~msLarge-scale training datasets
WEKA~400 GB/s (aggregate)~msCloud-native, POSIX-compatible
NFS/SMB~10 GB/s~ms⚠️ NOT for GPU training — too slow!

15.4 Power & Cooling — The 40kW+ Rack Challenge

A single DGX H100 draws 10.2 kW. A rack of 4 DGX systems = 40 kW — far exceeding traditional data center rack capacity (typically 5-15 kW). GPU clusters require fundamental rethinking of power distribution and cooling.

Why this matters for SREs: Most data centers were designed when a "high-density" rack drew 10 kW. GPU racks draw 4-5× that. This means: (1) you can't just plug a DGX into an existing rack — the power infrastructure (circuit breakers, PDUs, UPS) must be upgraded, (2) traditional air cooling (hot/cold aisle) maxes out at ~25 kW/rack — GPU racks require liquid cooling, and (3) the lead time for power/cooling upgrades can be 6-12 months in colocation facilities. Planning GPU infrastructure is a facilities project, not just an IT project. For anihpj: before ordering DGX systems, verify your data center can deliver 3-phase 415V power and has liquid cooling capability — or budget for a colocation provider that specializes in HPC/AI density.

🔌 Power Requirements

• DGX H100: 10.2 kW each
• 4× DGX per rack: 40-50 kW
• Requires 3-phase power (415V)
• UPS + generator for training continuity
• Budget: $10-15K/month per rack (power)

❄️ Cooling Solutions

• Air: Hot-aisle containment, max ~25 kW/rack
• Direct Liquid: Cold plates on GPUs/CPUs, ~50 kW/rack
• Immersion: Servers submerged in dielectric fluid, ~100 kW/rack
• DGX B200: Liquid cooling recommended

15.5 Cluster Sizing — How Many GPUs Do You Need?

Sizing a GPU cluster requires understanding your workload. The key metric: GPU-hours per training run. Multiply by the number of runs per day, add inference serving, and buffer for growth.

📝 Cluster Sizing Formula
Required GPUs = (Training GPU-hours/day + Inference GPU-hours/day) ÷ 24 × 1.3 (30% buffer)

Example: anihpj cluster
• Training: 2 DGX × 4 hrs/run × 1 run/day = 8 GPU-hrs × 8 GPUs/DGX = 64 GPU-hrs
• Inference: Need 4 GPUs 24/7 serving Triton = 96 GPU-hrs
• Total: (64 + 96) ÷ 24 × 1.3 = 8.7 → 12 GPUs minimum (round to 2× DGX H100)
• Future: Add 1 DGX for R&D = 3× DGX H100 recommended cluster

🚫 GPU Cluster Design Anti-Patterns — What NOT to Do

The NCA-AIIO exam tests your ability to identify bad design decisions. Here are the most common mistakes:

❌ Using NFS for Training Data

NFS maxes at ~10 GB/s per mount. A single DGX H100 needs 20+ GB/s to avoid GPU starvation. Use Lustre, WEKA, or GPUDirect Storage. NFS is a guaranteed bottleneck.

❌ 1:1 Oversubscription on IB Fabric

If 32 GPU nodes share one 400 GB/s IB switch, each GPU gets only 12.5 GB/s inter-node bandwidth — less than PCIe. Target non-blocking (1:1) or max 2:1 oversubscription.

❌ Mixing GPU Generations in One NCCL Ring

A100 and H100 in the same NCCL communicator forces the ring to run at the slowest GPU's speed. Keep training clusters homogeneous by GPU generation.

❌ Air Cooling 40kW+ Racks

Traditional hot/cold aisle air cooling maxes out at ~25 kW/rack. 4× DGX H100 = 40.8 kW. Requires liquid cooling — direct-to-chip or immersion.

✅ Design for Failure

Assume 1 GPU fails per week in a 100-GPU cluster. Design with: hot spare GPUs, checkpoint/resume, NCCL timeout configuration, and automated node cordoning via DCGM health checks.

✅ Right-Size Your Fabric

For training: non-blocking IB (1:1). For inference: 2:1-4:1 oversubscription acceptable. Formula: aggregate GPU BW / switch uplink BW = oversubscription ratio.

🏗️ GPU Cluster Topology — Fat-Tree vs Rail-Optimized

Two ways to connect GPU nodes. Fat-Tree = every node equal. Rail-Optimized = GPUs aligned by position across nodes for optimal all-reduce.

  FAT-TREE (General Purpose)              RAIL-OPTIMIZED (SuperPOD)
  ─────────────────────────              ──────────────────────────
  Spine switches connect all leaves        GPU[i] on every DGX connects to same leaf
  Full bisection bandwidth                 Optimized for NCCL ring all-reduce
  Best: inference, mixed workloads         Best: large-scale distributed training
  Overhead: more switches, higher cost     Efficient: 8 parallel "rails" operate independently
  For anihpj: 32-GPU cluster uses Fat-Tree for balanced training + inference

📝 NVIDIA Practice Questions — Chapter 15

Q1

What are the three tiers of a GPU cluster architecture?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Compute nodes (GPU servers), Network fabric (InfiniBand/Ethernet interconnect), and Storage nodes (NVMe/parallel filesystem). All three must be balanced — a slow storage tier starves GPUs, and a weak network limits distributed training scaling.

💡 EXPLANATION

Think of it as a three-legged stool — if any leg is too short, the whole thing falls. A cluster with 100 H100 GPUs and NFS storage will perform worse than 40 H100s with GPUDirect Storage, because the GPUs spend 60% of time idle waiting for data. Similarly, 8 DGX nodes on 100GbE instead of InfiniBand will see terrible multi-node scaling. The exam expects you to identify which tier is the bottleneck in a given scenario.

Q2

What is the bandwidth hierarchy for GPU communication?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

NVLink/NVSwitch (900 GB/s, intra-node) → InfiniBand NDR/XDR (400-800 GB/s, inter-node) → RoCE v2 (200-400 GB/s, Ethernet-based, lower cost). The goal is non-blocking fabric — no link should be oversubscribed.

💡 EXPLANATION
  GPU Communication Bandwidth Pyramid (Higher = Faster)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ▲ NVSwitch (900 GB/s) ← within 1 DGX node               │
  │  │ InfiniBand NDR (400 GB/s) ← between DGX nodes          │
  │  │ InfiniBand XDR (800 GB/s) ← next-gen (B200)            │
  │  │ RoCE v2 (200-400 GB/s) ← Ethernet, lower cost          │
  │  ▼ 100GbE (12.5 GB/s) ← NOT for training!                │
  │  Rule: intra-node BW should be 2-4× inter-node BW        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Q3

What is GPUDirect Storage and why is it important?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

GPUDirect Storage enables DMA transfers from NVMe storage directly into GPU memory, bypassing the CPU entirely. This eliminates the CPU as a bottleneck in the data pipeline and reduces latency from milliseconds to microseconds — critical for keeping GPUs fed during training.

💡 EXPLANATION

Without GPUDirect Storage, the data path is: NVMe → CPU RAM (via PCIe) → CPU copies → GPU RAM (via PCIe). Each hop costs latency and CPU cycles. With GPUDirect Storage: NVMe → GPU RAM (direct DMA). The CPU is completely bypassed — it can focus on other tasks. This is like having a dedicated loading dock for each GPU instead of making every delivery go through the main lobby.

Q4

Why is NFS not suitable for GPU training storage?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

NFS throughput (~10 GB/s) is far below what GPUs need (a single DGX H100 can consume ~20 GB/s). NFS introduces CPU overhead and latency that causes GPUs to stall waiting for data. Use local NVMe, GPUDirect Storage, Lustre, or WEKA instead.

💡 EXPLANATION

NFS is the #1 anti-pattern for AI storage. It's a single-threaded protocol designed for document sharing, not high-throughput parallel I/O. Even with NFSv4 + RDMA, you'll hit a wall at ~10-15 GB/s. A DGX H100 training a large model can consume 20-30 GB/s. The math is simple: if storage provides 10 GB/s but GPUs need 20 GB/s, GPUs are idle 50% of the time — you're burning electricity and GPU depreciation for nothing. Always use parallel filesystems (Lustre/WEKA) or GPUDirect Storage for training clusters.

Q5

What power does a rack of 4 DGX H100 systems require?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

40-50 kW (4 × 10.2 kW per DGX, plus networking and storage). This requires 3-phase 415V power and liquid cooling (direct-to-chip or immersion). Traditional air-cooled data centers (5-15 kW per rack) cannot support this density.

💡 EXPLANATION

This is the "oh wait, we can't actually power this" question that trips up infrastructure planners. A typical enterprise data center rack is designed for 5-15 kW with 208V single-phase power. A DGX rack needs 40-50 kW and 415V 3-phase — you literally cannot plug it into a standard rack PDU. Before ordering DGX systems, you must: (1) verify electrical infrastructure (breaker capacity, 415V availability), (2) plan liquid cooling loops (direct-to-chip or rear-door heat exchangers), (3) budget 6-12 months for facility upgrades in colocation.

Q6

What is the difference between fat-tree and rail-optimized network topologies?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Fat-tree: Full bisection bandwidth — every node has equal BW to every other node. General purpose. Rail-optimized: GPUs at the same position across nodes share a dedicated rail, optimized for all-reduce communication patterns in distributed training. More efficient for AI workloads but less flexible.

💡 EXPLANATION

In a 32-node cluster, fat-tree ensures Node 0→Node 31 has the same bandwidth as Node 0→Node 1. This is ideal but expensive (many switches). Rail-optimized topology assigns GPU 0 in every node to Rail 0, GPU 1 to Rail 1, etc. During all-reduce, each GPU communicates primarily within its rail — reducing cross-rail traffic. This matches NCCL's ring algorithm perfectly. Rail-optimized is the standard for DGX SuperPOD because it's more cost-effective at scale while matching AI communication patterns.

Q7

How do you calculate the required number of GPUs for a cluster?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Required GPUs = (Training GPU-hrs/day + Inference GPU-hrs/day) ÷ 24 × 1.3. The 1.3 factor is a 30% buffer for growth, maintenance, and unexpected workloads. GPU-hours = nodes × GPUs per node × hours used.

💡 EXPLANATION

The 1.3 buffer factor is not arbitrary — it accounts for: (1) one node down for maintenance/repair at any time (~8% overhead), (2) peak load spikes (~15% headroom), (3) future model growth (~7% buffer). For the exam: if a question gives you GPU-hours and asks for cluster size, divide by 24, multiply by 1.3, and round up to the nearest whole GPU. Don't forget to express the answer in DGX/HGX node counts (divide by 8 for DGX).

Q8

What is NCCL and what does it optimize?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) optimizes collective operations (all-reduce, all-gather, broadcast, reduce-scatter) across GPUs. It automatically selects the best communication path (NVLink within node, InfiniBand across nodes) and uses ring/tree algorithms for maximum bandwidth. Essential for distributed training.

💡 EXPLANATION

NCCL is the invisible hero of GPU clusters. When PyTorch calls torch.distributed.all_reduce(gradients), NCCL figures out: (1) which GPUs are on the same NVSwitch domain (use NVLink), (2) which are on different nodes (use InfiniBand), (3) the optimal ring order to minimize hops. Without NCCL, every framework would need to implement this themselves. NCCL is why distributed training "just works" on NVIDIA hardware — it abstracts away the entire communication topology.

Q9

What is the recommended anihpj GPU cluster design?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

3× DGX H100 (2 for training, 1 for R&D) + 1× DGX Station (dev) + 2× HGX H100 servers (inference). Network: Quantum-2 IB. Storage: 200 TB WEKA. Power: ~60 kW, liquid cooled. Total: ~$2.5M initial, ~$250K/yr operational. Break-even vs cloud in ~18 months.

💡 EXPLANATION

This design balances cost, performance, and flexibility. The 2 training DGX handle 95% of workload; the 3rd DGX is for R&D experimentation without competing for training resources. The DGX Station enables local prototyping before cluster-scale training. The 2 HGX inference nodes are from Dell/HPE — cheaper than DGX and integrate with existing DC management. The 18-month cloud break-even assumes: $98/hr × 24/7/365 = $858K/yr cloud cost for equivalent 8×H100 capacity. $2.5M / $858K = 2.9 years, but factoring reserved instances (40% off) and spot (70% off), break-even is ~18 months.

Q10

What cooling technology is recommended for DGX B200 and why?

Click to reveal answer
✅ ANSWER

Direct liquid cooling (cold plates on GPUs and CPUs). DGX B200 draws ~14 kW (vs 10.2 kW for H100) — beyond what air cooling can efficiently handle in a rack. Liquid cooling removes ~90% of heat directly at the source, enabling higher density and lower PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness).

💡 EXPLANATION

The trend is clear: each GPU generation draws more power. A100: 400W, H100: 700W, B200: 1000W per GPU. At 8 GPUs + CPU + networking, DGX B200 hits ~14 kW. Air cooling requires enormous airflow (loud, energy-hungry fans) and struggles beyond ~25 kW/rack due to physics — you can't move enough air through a rack. Liquid cooling is 3,500× more efficient at heat removal than air (water's thermal capacity vs air's). The exam expects you to associate B200 with liquid cooling.

Chapter 16: TensorRT — High-Performance Inference🔴 Advanced

Chapter 16: TensorRT — Making AI Models Run at Warp Speed

TensorRT is NVIDIA's inference optimization engine that takes a trained model and transforms it into the fastest possible version for your specific GPU. It applies layer fusion, precision calibration, and kernel auto-tuning to achieve 5-10× faster inference than raw PyTorch/TensorFlow — with minimal accuracy loss. For anihpj jobpost, TensorRT accelerates the job matching model to serve thousands of candidates per second on Triton.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours⚡ Optimization🚀 Inference

🧑‍🏫 TensorRT Explained: Like a JIT Compiler for AI Models

Raw PyTorch is like an interpreter — it reads your model code and executes each operation step-by-step. TensorRT is like a compiler — it analyzes the entire model graph, fuses operations together, chooses the fastest GPU instructions, and produces an optimized binary (.plan file). The result runs 5-10× faster with half the memory.

Three Optimizations: (1) Layer Fusion — merges Conv+BN+ReLU into ONE GPU kernel (eliminates 3 memory read/write cycles). (2) Precision Calibration — reduces 32-bit numbers to 16-bit or 8-bit (half/fourth the memory, 2-4× faster). (3) Kernel Auto-Tuning — tests hundreds of GPU instruction variants and picks the fastest for YOUR specific GPU model.

Critical Fact: TensorRT engines are GPU-specific. An engine built for A100 won't run on H100. You rebuild per GPU architecture. For anihpj: 1 GPU with TRT INT8 handles 3000+ req/sec — the work of ~30 GPUs running raw PyTorch.

🆕 TensorRT 11.0 (2026): Strongly-typed networks now default (weak-typing APIs removed). Multi-Device Inference is GA with AllToAll/Gather/Scatter collective ops. Ragged batching for attention (packed variable-length sequences). MoE inference majorly improved on Blackwell. Migrate custom plugins from IPluginV2 to IPluginV3.

🎯 NCA-AIIO: AI Infrastructure ~35% 🎯 NCA-AIIO: AI Operations ~30%

  • Learn the three optimization pillars: layer fusion, precision calibration, kernel tuning

  • Build and serialize a TensorRT engine from a PyTorch model
  • Use TensorRT-LLM for optimized LLM inference

🔑 Exam Tip — TensorRT

The NCA-AIIO exam tests TensorRT knowledge: FP16 → 2-3×, INT8 → 4-5×, plus fusion → 5-10× total. Know that TensorRT engines are GPU-specific (an A100 engine won't run on H100). Understand the ONNX workflow: PyTorch → ONNX → TensorRT. Expect 3-4 questions, especially around quantization and engine building.

16.1 What is TensorRT?

TensorRT is NVIDIA's SDK for high-performance deep learning inference. It takes a trained model from any framework (PyTorch, TensorFlow, ONNX) and applies aggressive optimizations to maximize inference speed on NVIDIA GPUs. The key insight: training and inference are fundamentally different workloads. Training needs flexibility (autograd, dynamic graphs). Inference needs raw speed — the model structure is fixed, weights are frozen, and precision can be reduced. TensorRT is built specifically for this inference-only scenario.

TensorRT works by compiling your model into an optimized representation: parsing the model graph, fusing layers together, selecting the fastest GPU kernels for each operation, and optionally quantizing to lower precision. The output is a serialized engine (.trt or .plan file) that loads in milliseconds and runs at maximum GPU efficiency. For anihpj: convert the PyTorch job matching model → ONNX → TensorRT engine → deploy on Triton. Inference latency drops from ~5ms to ~1ms — critical when serving 1000+ requests per second.

Why this matters for the exam: The NCA-AIIO certification tests your understanding of the inference optimization pipeline. You need to know that TensorRT is NOT a training tool — it's purely for inference. You need to understand that engines are GPU-specific (an A100 engine won't run on H100). And you need to know the three optimization pillars: layer fusion (merging ops to eliminate memory traffic), precision calibration (FP32→FP16→INT8 for speed), and kernel auto-tuning (selecting optimal CUDA kernels for your specific GPU architecture). These three together deliver the 5-10× speedup that makes TensorRT essential for production AI deployments.

16.2 Model Optimization — Layer Fusion, Precision Calibration, Kernel Tuning

TensorRT Optimization Pipeline
