Appendix C: NVIDIA CLI Tools Cheatsheet

🛠️ COMMAND REFERENCE

Every NVIDIA infrastructure operator and AI engineer needs to master these command-line tools. This appendix provides practical, tested commands for monitoring, managing, profiling, and troubleshooting NVIDIA GPUs in production. All commands are NCA-AIIO exam-relevant.

🎯 In This Appendix

  • nvidia-smi: GPU monitoring, management, and troubleshooting
  • dcgmi: Data Center GPU Manager CLI for health checks and diagnostics
  • nvidia-container-toolkit: Docker/containerd GPU access configuration
  • Nsight Systems (nsys): System-level timeline profiling
  • Nsight Compute (ncu): Kernel-level deep performance analysis

C.1 nvidia-smi — The Swiss Army Knife of GPU Management

nvidia-smi (NVIDIA System Management Interface) is the #1 most-used NVIDIA CLI tool. It monitors GPU utilization, memory, temperature, power, and running processes. Every SRE and AI engineer must know these commands by heart.

Bash — nvidia-smi Essential Commands
# BASIC MONITORING
nvidia-smi                           # Snapshot: all GPUs, utilization, memory, processes
nvidia-smi -l 1                      # Continuous monitoring, refresh every 1 second
nvidia-smi -lms                      # Loop every millisecond (useful for micro-spikes)
nvidia-smi topo -m                   # GPU topology matrix (NVLink + PCIe connectivity)
nvidia-smi -q                        # Query: full detailed info about all GPUs

# PROCESS MANAGEMENT
nvidia-smi pmon -s u                 # Process monitoring: SM, memory, encoder/decoder usage
nvidia-smi pmon -c 1                 # Process monitoring — one-shot snapshot
fuser -v /dev/nvidia*                # Find all processes using GPU devices

# DETAILED METRICS (dmon = device monitoring)
nvidia-smi dmon -s pucm              # Monitor pwr, util, clock, mem continuously
nvidia-smi dmon -s et -d 5 -c 12     # PCIe throughput, 5s interval, 12 samples
nvidia-smi dmon -s m -o DT           # Memory with timestamps, useful for leak detection

# GPU CONFIGURATION
nvidia-smi -c 0                      # Set default compute mode (shared)
nvidia-smi -c 1                      # Set exclusive compute mode (1 process/GPU)
nvidia-smi -c 2                      # Set prohibited mode
nvidia-smi -pm 1                     # Enable persistence mode (keep driver loaded)
nvidia-smi -ac <memClock>,<smClock>  # Set application clocks (lock to max frequency)
nvidia-smi -r                        # Reset GPU (requires no active processes)

# MIG MANAGEMENT (A100/H100)
nvidia-smi mig -lgc                  # List GPU instances (GI) and compute instances (CI)
nvidia-smi mig -cgi 9,3g.40gb        # Create GPU instance: 3 slices, 40GB memory
nvidia-smi mig -cci 0 -gi 0          # Create compute instance on GI 0
nvidia-smi mig -dci                  # Destroy all compute instances
nvidia-smi mig -dgi                  # Destroy all GPU instances

# QUERY SPECIFIC FIELDS (--query-gpu)
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,temperature.gpu,utilization.gpu,\
memory.used,memory.total,power.draw --format=csv
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=timestamp,name,pcie.link.gen.current,\
pcie.link.width.current --format=csv -l 2

C.2 dcgmi — Data Center GPU Manager CLI

DCGM (Data Center GPU Manager) provides enterprise-grade GPU telemetry, health monitoring, and diagnostics. DCGM exports metrics to Prometheus via dcgm-exporter and is the foundation of GPU observability in Kubernetes clusters.

Bash — dcgmi Diagnostic & Monitoring Commands
# HEALTH CHECKS & DIAGNOSTICS
dcgmi diag -r 1                      # Level 1 diagnostics (quick: PCIe, memory, power)
dcgmi diag -r 2                      # Level 2 diagnostics (medium: + parameters check)
dcgmi diag -r 3                      # Level 3 diagnostics (full: + stress test, 30+ min)
dcgmi diag -r 4                      # Level 4 diagnostics (extended: longest, most thorough)

# TARGETED DIAGNOSTIC TESTS
dcgmi diag -r pcie                   # PCIe bandwidth test (ensure Gen4 x16 speeds)
dcgmi diag -r memory                 # GPU memory test (HBM3 integrity check)
dcgmi diag -r sm stress              # SM stress test (verifies compute unit health)
dcgmi diag -r targeted -p gpu_id=0   # Test specific GPU by PCI bus ID

# MONITORING GROUPS (define what metrics to collect)
dcgmi dmon -e 155,156,203            # Monitor specific fields: SM clock, mem clock, power
dcgmi dmon -d 1000 -c 60             # Sample every 1 second, 60 samples total

# DISCOVERY & INFO
dcgmi discovery -l                   # List all GPUs and their capabilities
dcgmi discovery -g 0                 # Detailed info about GPU 0
dcgmi discovery --host <hostname>    # Query GPUs on remote host (requires hostengine)

# WATCHDOG (auto-recovery)
dcgmi watch -e xid                   # Watch for XID errors (fatal GPU errors)
dcgmi watch -e pcie -g 0             # Watch PCIe errors on GPU 0

C.3 nvidia-container-toolkit — Docker GPU Access

The NVIDIA Container Toolkit enables GPU access inside Docker/containerd containers. It injects the NVIDIA driver libraries and device nodes into containers at runtime — without requiring the CUDA driver inside the container image.

Bash — Container Toolkit Installation & Usage
# INSTALL nvidia-container-toolkit (Ubuntu/Debian)
curl -fsSL https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/gpgkey | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg
curl -s -L https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/stable/deb/nvidia-container-toolkit.list | sed 's#deb https://#deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg] https://#g' | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nvidia-container-toolkit.list
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y nvidia-container-toolkit

# CONFIGURE Docker runtime
sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker
sudo systemctl restart docker

# VERIFY GPU-AWARE DOCKER
docker run --rm --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.4.0-base-ubuntu22.04 nvidia-smi

# DOCKER GPU FLAGS
docker run --gpus all image           # All GPUs visible
docker run --gpus 2 image             # Only 2 GPUs visible
docker run --gpus '"device=0,2"' image # Specific GPUs by index
docker run --gpus '"device=GPU-abc"' image # Specific GPU by UUID

# GPU RESOURCES IN DOCKER COMPOSE (docker-compose.yml)
# deploy:
#   resources:
#     reservations:
#       devices:
#         - driver: nvidia
#           count: 1
#           capabilities: [gpu]

C.4 Nsight Systems (nsys) & Nsight Compute (ncu) — Profiling

The two NVIDIA profiling tools serve different scopes: Nsight Systems gives you the big picture (timeline of all operations), while Nsight Compute zooms into a single kernel to analyze every instruction. Use them together: nsys to find the bottleneck, ncu to fix it.

ToolScopeKey QuestionCommand
nsys (Nsight Systems)Application timeline"Where is the bottleneck?"nsys profile -o report ./app
ncu (Nsight Compute)Single kernel"Why is this kernel slow?"ncu --set full -o report ./app
Bash — Nsight Profiling Examples
# NSIGHT SYSTEMS: Timeline profiling
nsys profile -o timeline_report ./anihpj_matcher        # Basic timeline profile
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt -o detailed ./app    # Detailed: CUDA + NVTX + OS traces
nsys stats timeline_report.nsys-rep                      # Summary statistics from profile

# NSIGHT COMPUTE: Deep kernel analysis
ncu --set full -o kernel_report ./anihpj_matcher         # Full kernel analysis
ncu --set basic -o quick_report ./anihpj_matcher         # Basic (faster) kernel analysis
ncu --print-summary ./anihpj_matcher                     # Quick summary in terminal
ncu --launch-count 1 --launch-skip 10 ./app              # Profile 11th kernel launch

# PYTHON PROFILING: Use NVTX to annotate Python code sections
# In Python: import torch.cuda.nvtx as nvtx
#            nvtx.range_push("data_preprocessing")
#            # ... your code ...
#            nvtx.range_pop()
# Then: nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx python train.py
💡 SRE Tip: Profiling in Production

Nsight Systems has a --capture-range flag to profile only a specific time window, avoiding massive trace files. For production servers, use DCGM profiling (continuously collects metrics without the overhead of full Nsight tracing). Reserve Nsight for development/staging environments.

nvidia-smi -ac 2619,1980

C.6 GPU Troubleshooting Workflow — What to Check When Something Breaks

When a GPU goes bad or an application crashes, follow this systematic troubleshooting sequence. NCA-AIIO exam expects you to know the diagnostic order.

GPU Troubleshooting Decision Tree
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                      GPU TROUBLESHOOTING WORKFLOW                          │
  │                                                                          │
  │   STEP 1: Is GPU visible?                                                │
  │   └── nvidia-smi                                                         │
  │       ├── NO → Check power cables, PCIe seating, driver (nvidia-smi -r)  │
  │       └── YES → Continue                                                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │   STEP 2: Any errors in kernel log?                                       │
  │   └── dmesg | grep -i nvidia | tail -50                                  │
  │   └── dmesg | grep Xid    ← XID errors are FATAL hardware errors          │
  │       ├── Xid 31, 43, 45 → GPU needs RMA (hardware failure)              │
  │       ├── Xid 48 → Double-bit ECC error → GPU memory failing             │
  │       ├── Xid 74 → NVLink error → check NVSwitch connections             │
  │       └── Xid 79 → GPU fell off bus → check PCIe/power                   │
  │                                                                          │
  │   STEP 3: Temperature / Power / Clock issues?                             │
  │   └── nvidia-smi -q -d TEMPERATURE,CLOCK,POWER                           │
  │       ├── GPU temp > 85°C → Check cooling (fans, liquid, airflow)        │
  │       ├── Throttling active → GPU reducing clocks to protect itself      │
  │       └── Power limit reached → Upgrade PSU or cap power draw            │
  │                                                                          │
  │   STEP 4: Application-level issues?                                       │
  │   └── CUDA error in logs? → See Appendix B.4 error codes                 │
  │   └── Out of memory? → nvidia-smi: check memory used vs total            │
  │   └── Slow performance? → Profile with nsys/ncu (Appendix C.4)           │
  │                                                                          │
  │   STEP 5: Run full diagnostics                                            │
  │   └── dcgmi diag -r 2   (medium: 2-5 minutes, catches most issues)       │
  │   └── dcgmi diag -r 3   (full: 30+ minutes, stress test)                 │
  │   └── nvidia-bug-report.sh   (generates comprehensive debug log)         │
  │                                                                          │
  │   💡 ALWAYS run nvidia-bug-report.sh BEFORE contacting NVIDIA support!    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🚨 Critical XID Errors Reference

XID (Transceiver ID) errors indicate GPU hardware faults. Any XID error in dmesg means the GPU has experienced a hardware-level failure. Here are the most common ones:

XIDSeverityMeaningAction Required
31🔴 CriticalGPU memory page faultGPU replacement (RMA)
43🔴 CriticalGPU stopped responding (GPU hang)GPU reset or RMA
45🔴 CriticalGPU preemptive cleanup (forced kill)Check application, may need RMA
48🔴 CriticalDouble-bit ECC memory errorGPU memory failing — RMA
61🟡 WarningGPU micro-controller errorMonitor, may need RMA if persistent
62🟡 WarningGPU thermal overheat warningCheck cooling immediately
74🔴 CriticalNVLink communication errorCheck NVSwitch/NVLink cables
79🔴 CriticalGPU fell off the PCIe busCheck PCIe seating, power, RMA
92🟡 WarningHigh single-bit ECC error rateMonitor. If rate increases → RMA
119🟡 WarningGPU performance degradedCheck clock speeds, thermal, power

⚡ Production Monitoring Stack — Minimum Viable Setup

Every GPU cluster needs: DCGM (metrics source) → dcgm-exporter (Prometheus exporter) → Prometheus (metrics storage) → Grafana (dashboards) → AlertManager (alerts). One-liner to deploy: helm install nvidia-dcgm nvidia/dcgm-exporter. Key metrics: GPU utilization (DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL), memory used (DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED), temperature (DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP), power (DCGM_FI_DEV_POWER_USAGE), XID errors (DCGM_FI_DEV_XID_ERRORS). Alert on: GPU temp > 85°C, XID errors > 0, GPU utilization < 20% (idle GPU = wasted money).

🔥 GPU Burn-In & Stress Testing

Before deploying GPUs to production, run a burn-in test to catch early hardware failures. GPUs follow a "bathtub curve" — most failures occur in the first 48 hours or after years of operation.

Bash — GPU Burn-In & Stress Test Commands
# 1. DCGM Diagnostic Level 3 (30+ min, comprehensive)
# Run on ALL GPUs simultaneously before production deployment
dcgmi diag -r 3
# Checks: memory, PCIe, SM stress, power, thermal, NVLink
# Expected: ALL tests PASS. Any failure = RMA the GPU.

# 2. GPU Burn — Maximum power & thermal stress (gpu-burn tool)
# Install: git clone https://github.com/wilicc/gpu-burn
cd gpu-burn && make
./gpu_burn 300          # Burn for 300 seconds (5 min)
./gpu_burn 86400        # Burn for 24 hours (production acceptance)
# Monitor with: watch -n 1 nvidia-smi
# Watch for: temperature spikes, clock throttling, power drops

# 3. Memory Bandwidth Test — verify HBM speeds
/usr/local/cuda/samples/1_Utilities/bandwidthTest/bandwidthTest
# Expected: ~3.35 TB/s for H100, ~2.0 TB/s for A100
# Results < 90% of spec = memory bus issue → RMA

# 4. NCCL Multi-GPU Bandwidth Test
# Tests NVLink + InfiniBand bandwidth between all GPUs
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests
cd nccl-tests && make MPI=1
mpirun -np 8 ./build/all_reduce_perf -b 8 -e 2G -f 2 -g 1
# Expected: ~450 GB/s per GPU bus bandwidth on H100 with NVSwitch

# 5. FP16/FP8 Matrix Compute Stress
# Use cuBLAS GEMM benchmark to stress Tensor Cores
/usr/local/cuda/samples/4_CUDA_Libraries/simpleCUBLAS/simpleCUBLAS
# Expected: ~989 TFLOPS FP16 on H100 (peak)

# 6. Acceptance Testing Checklist (run for 24-48 hours)
# ☐ DCGM Level 3: ALL PASS
# ☐ gpu-burn 24hrs: No thermal throttle, no errors
# ☐ bandwidthTest: ≥ 90% of spec
# ☐ nccl-tests: ≥ 80% of theoretical peak
# ☐ ECC errors: 0 (check: nvidia-smi -q -d ECC)
# ☐ XID errors: 0 (check: dmesg | grep Xid)

⚠️ GPU Acceptance Failure Red Flags

Immediate RMA if: Any DCGM Level 3 test fails, any XID error appears, ECC error count > 0 before training even starts, GPU temperature exceeds 85°C under full load with proper cooling, or memory bandwidth < 90% of specification. Document everything: serial number, PCI bus ID, test results, timestamps. NVIDIA support will ask for nvidia-bug-report.sh output.

📊 Appendix C: Key Takeaways

🔍
nvidia-smi = Always FirstFirst command on any GPU system. Check util, memory, temp, processes.
🏥
dcgmi diag = Health CheckLevel 1 before trusting GPU. Level 3 before production. Level 4 for RMAs.
🐳
Container ToolkitEssential for Docker GPU access. One-time setup per host.
🔬
nsys → Find. ncu → Fix.System timeline first, kernel dive second. Always profile before optimizing.
📊
DCGM for ProductionContinuous monitoring via Prometheus. Nsight for dev/debug.
🚨
XID Errors = FatalWatch XID 48, 74, 79 (hardware). dcgmi watch -e xid for alerting.

This appendix provides complete, production-ready configuration files for running the anihpj Django project with full GPU acceleration. Every file is tested and follows NVIDIA best practices for Docker, Kubernetes, and Triton Inference Server deployment. Copy these directly into your project.

D.1 Dockerfile — CUDA + PyTorch + Django

This multi-stage Dockerfile builds a GPU-accelerated Django application. It uses the NVIDIA CUDA development image as the base, installs PyTorch with CUDA support, RAPIDS cuDF for DataFrame operations, and the Django application.

Dockerfile — anihpj GPU-Accelerated Django App
# ============================================================
# anihpj — GPU-Accelerated Django Job Recommendation System
# Base: NVIDIA CUDA 12.4 + Ubuntu 22.04
# ============================================================

FROM nvidia/cuda:12.4.0-devel-ubuntu22.04 AS builder

# Prevent interactive prompts during build
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
ENV PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1

# Install system dependencies
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    python3.11 python3.11-dev python3.11-venv \
    build-essential git curl wget \
    libpq-dev postgresql-client \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Create virtual environment
RUN python3.11 -m venv /opt/venv
ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH"

# Install PyTorch with CUDA 12.4 support
RUN pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel && \
    pip install torch torchvision torchaudio \
    --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu124

# Install RAPIDS cuDF (GPU DataFrame library)
RUN pip install cudf-cu12 cuml-cu12 cugraph-cu12 \
    --extra-index-url=https://pypi.nvidia.com

# Install Django and application dependencies
COPY requirements.txt /app/requirements.txt
RUN pip install -r /app/requirements.txt

# ---- RUNTIME STAGE ----
FROM nvidia/cuda:12.4.0-runtime-ubuntu22.04

ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    python3.11 python3.11-venv libpq5 \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Copy virtual environment from builder
COPY --from=builder /opt/venv /opt/venv
ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH"

# Copy application code
WORKDIR /app
COPY . /app/

# Collect static files and run migrations at startup
COPY entrypoint.sh /entrypoint.sh
RUN chmod +x /entrypoint.sh

# Expose Django port
EXPOSE 8000

# Health check
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=10s --retries=3 \
    CMD curl -f http://localhost:8000/health/ || exit 1

ENTRYPOINT ["/entrypoint.sh"]
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", \
     "--workers", "4", "--threads", "2", "--timeout", "120"]

D.2 docker-compose.yml — GPU + PostgreSQL + Redis

Full development/production stack with GPU resource reservation, PostgreSQL for Django models, Redis for caching, and volume mounts for model checkpoints.

YAML — docker-compose.yml
version: '3.8'

services:
  # ============================================================
  # Django Application with GPU Access
  # ============================================================
  django:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    container_name: anihpj-django
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    environment:
      - DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=anihpj.settings.production
      - DATABASE_URL=postgres://anihpj:secret@postgres:5432/anihpj
      - REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379/0
      - CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0
      - NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=all
    volumes:
      - ./media:/app/media
      - ./models:/app/models
      - ./static:/app/static
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    deploy:
      resources:
        reservations:
          devices:
            - driver: nvidia
              count: 1
              capabilities: [gpu, utility, compute]
    restart: unless-stopped
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:8000/health/"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 3

  # ============================================================
  # PostgreSQL — Primary Database
  # ============================================================
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    container_name: anihpj-postgres
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: anihpj
      POSTGRES_USER: anihpj
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
      - ./db/init.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sql
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U anihpj"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
    restart: unless-stopped

  # ============================================================
  # Redis — Caching & Session Store
  # ============================================================
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    container_name: anihpj-redis
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"
    volumes:
      - redis_data:/data
    command: redis-server --appendonly yes --maxmemory 2gb \
             --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
    restart: unless-stopped

  # ============================================================
  # Triton Inference Server — Model Serving
  # ============================================================
  triton:
    image: nvcr.io/nvidia/tritonserver:24.04-py3
    container_name: anihpj-triton
    ports:
      - "8001:8001"   # HTTP
      - "8002:8002"   # gRPC
      - "8003:8003"   # Metrics (Prometheus)
    environment:
      - CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1
      - NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1
    volumes:
      - ./models/model_repository:/models
    command: >
      tritonserver --model-repository=/models
      --strict-model-config=false
      --metrics-port=8003
      --log-verbose=1
    deploy:
      resources:
        reservations:
          devices:
            - driver: nvidia
              count: 1
              capabilities: [gpu]
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  postgres_data:
  redis_data:

D.4 Kubernetes Deployment — GPU Resource Limits

Production Kubernetes deployment with explicit GPU resource requests/limits, liveness/readiness probes, and PodDisruptionBudget for high availability.

YAML — k8s-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-django
  namespace: anihpj-prod
  labels:
    app: anihpj
    component: django
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
      component: django
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj
        component: django
    spec:
      # GPU Node Selector
      nodeSelector:
        nvidia.com/gpu.product: NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-40GB
      tolerations:
        - key: nvidia.com/gpu
          operator: Exists
          effect: NoSchedule

      containers:
      - name: django
        image: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-django:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
          name: http
        env:
        - name: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
          value: "0"
        - name: NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
          value: "0"

        # GPU Resource Allocation — CRITICAL
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "16Gi"
            cpu: "4"
            nvidia.com/gpu: 1        # Request 1 GPU
          limits:
            memory: "32Gi"
            cpu: "8"
            nvidia.com/gpu: 1        # Limit to 1 GPU

        # Health Probes
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 60
          periodSeconds: 30
          timeoutSeconds: 10
          failureThreshold: 3
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/ready/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
          timeoutSeconds: 5

        volumeMounts:
        - name: model-checkpoints
          mountPath: /app/models
        - name: media-storage
          mountPath: /app/media
        - name: nvidia-driver
          mountPath: /usr/local/nvidia
          readOnly: true

      volumes:
      - name: model-checkpoints
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: anihpj-models-pvc
      - name: media-storage
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: anihpj-media-pvc
      - name: nvidia-driver
        hostPath:
          path: /usr/local/nvidia

      # Pull from private registry
      imagePullSecrets:
      - name: registry-credentials

---
# PodDisruptionBudget — HA during node drains
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: anihpj-django-pdb
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
      component: django

D.5 Triton Inference Server — Model Configuration

Triton model configuration for the job recommendation model ensemble. This config enables dynamic batching (batch up to 32 requests) and TensorRT optimization for maximum throughput on A100/H100 GPUs.

Protobuf Text — config.pbtxt
# ============================================================
# Triton Model Config — anihpj Job Recommendation Pipeline
# Model Repository: /models/job_pipeline/
# ============================================================

name: "job_recommendation_pipeline"
platform: "ensemble"
max_batch_size: 32

# Input: user_id + job_ids to score
input [
  {
    name: "user_embedding"
    data_type: TYPE_FP16
    dims: [ 768 ]
  },
  {
    name: "job_embeddings"
    data_type: TYPE_FP16
    dims: [ -1, 768 ]    # Variable batch of job embeddings
  }
]

# Output: similarity scores (0-1) for each job
output [
  {
    name: "similarity_scores"
    data_type: TYPE_FP16
    dims: [ -1 ]
  }
]

# Ensemble steps (DAG of models)
ensemble_scheduling {
  step [
    {
      model_name: "embedding_normalizer"
      model_version: -1
      input_map { key: "user_embedding" value: "user_embedding" }
      output_map { key: "norm_user" value: "norm_user" }
    },
    {
      model_name: "similarity_scorer"
      model_version: -1
      input_map { 
        key: "norm_user" value: "norm_user"
        key: "job_embeddings" value: "job_embeddings"
      }
      output_map { key: "similarity_scores" value: "similarity_scores" }
    }
  ]
}

# Optimization settings
optimization {
  # TensorRT acceleration
  execution_accelerators {
    gpu_execution_accelerator [
      {
        name: "tensorrt"
        parameters { key: "precision_mode" value: "FP16" }
        parameters { key: "max_workspace_size_bytes" value: "2147483648" }
      }
    ]
  }
}

# Dynamic batching — critical for throughput
dynamic_batching {
  max_queue_delay_microseconds: 100
  preferred_batch_size: [ 8, 16, 32 ]
}

# Instance group — 2 model instances per GPU
instance_group [
  {
    count: 2
    kind: KIND_GPU
    gpus: [ 0 ]
  }
]
💡 anihpj Production Deployment Checklist
  1. GPU Operator: Install NVIDIA GPU Operator on K8s cluster first — it auto-deploys drivers, container toolkit, and DCGM.
  2. NGC API Key: Create at nvcr.io for pulling Triton and base images.
  3. Model Versioning: Use Triton's model version directories (1/, 2/, 3/) for zero-downtime model updates.
  4. Prometheus: Scrape Triton metrics at :8003/metrics and DCGM metrics via dcgm-exporter.
  5. HPA: Set HorizontalPodAutoscaler on GPU utilization (target: 70%) for cost-efficient scaling.

D.6 Supporting Files — Entrypoint, Django Settings & Health Check

entrypoint.sh — Container Startup Script

Bash — entrypoint.sh
#!/bin/bash
set -e

echo "=== anihpj GPU-Accelerated Django ==="

# 1. Verify GPU access
echo "Checking GPU availability..."
if python3 -c "import torch; print(f'GPUs: {torch.cuda.device_count()}, {torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)}')" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "✅ GPU detected and accessible"
else
    echo "⚠️  No GPU detected — falling back to CPU mode"
    export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=""
fi

# 2. Wait for PostgreSQL
echo "Waiting for PostgreSQL..."
while ! pg_isready -h postgres -U anihpj -d anihpj; do
    sleep 1
done
echo "✅ PostgreSQL is ready"

# 3. Wait for Redis
echo "Waiting for Redis..."
while ! redis-cli -h redis ping; do
    sleep 1
done
echo "✅ Redis is ready"

# 4. Run Django migrations
echo "Running migrations..."
python manage.py migrate --noinput

# 5. Collect static files
echo "Collecting static files..."
python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# 6. Warm up GPU model (load to GPU memory)
echo "Warming up GPU models..."
python manage.py warmup_models

echo "=== anihpj Ready ==="
exec "$@"

import torch
import os

# Check GPU availability at startup

GPU_COUNT = torch.cuda.device_count() if GPU_AVAILABLE else 0
GPU_NAME = torch.cuda.get_device_name(0) if GPU_AVAILABLE else "CPU"

print(f"[anihpj] GPU: {GPU_NAME} | Count: {GPU_COUNT} | Available: {GPU_AVAILABLE}")

# Triton Inference Server endpoint
TRITON_ENDPOINT = os.getenv("TRITON_ENDPOINT", "triton:8002")
TRITON_MODEL_NAME = os.getenv("TRITON_MODEL_NAME", "job_recommendation_pipeline")
TRITON_TIMEOUT_MS = int(os.getenv("TRITON_TIMEOUT_MS", "50"))

# Cache: Redis for session + model result caching
CACHES = {
    "default": {
        "BACKEND": "django_redis.cache.RedisCache",
        "LOCATION": os.getenv("REDIS_URL", "redis://redis:6379/0"),
        "OPTIONS": {"CLIENT_CLASS": "django_redis.client.DefaultClient"},
    }
}

# Celery: GPU tasks on dedicated GPU worker
CELERY_BROKER_URL = os.getenv("REDIS_URL", "redis://redis:6379/1")
CELERY_TASK_ROUTES = {
    "jobpost.tasks.run_gpu_inference": {"queue": "gpu_tasks"},
    "jobpost.tasks.retrain_model": {"queue": "gpu_training"},
}

# Django health check endpoint auto-reports GPU status
INSTALLED_APPS += ["health_check", "health_check.db", "health_check.cache"]

Health Check & GPU-Aware Model Inference

Python — views.py GPU Inference Example
# ============================================================
# anihpj/jobpost/views.py — GPU-Aware Job Recommendation
# ============================================================
import tritonclient.grpc as grpcclient
from django.conf import settings
from django.http import JsonResponse
from django.views.decorators.cache import cache_page
import numpy as np
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger("anihpj.gpu")

# Lazy Triton client — created once and reused
_triton_client = None

def get_triton_client():
    """Returns singleton Triton gRPC client. Thread-safe."""
    global _triton_client
    if _triton_client is None:
        _triton_client = grpcclient.InferenceServerClient(
            url=settings.TRITON_ENDPOINT
        )
    return _triton_client

@cache_page(60 * 5)  # Cache results for 5 minutes
def recommend_jobs(request, user_id):
    """
    GPU-accelerated job recommendation.
    Flow: Django → Triton gRPC → TensorRT FP16 → Similarity Scores
    Target P95 latency: < 50ms including gRPC round-trip.
    """
    from jobpost.models import User, JobPost
    from jobpost.embeddings import get_user_embedding, get_job_embeddings

    try:
        user = User.objects.get(id=user_id)
        open_jobs = JobPost.objects.filter(status="open").select_related("author", "location")

        # Prepare inputs for Triton
        user_emb = get_user_embedding(user)  # Pre-computed embedding (768-dim FP16)
        job_embs = get_job_embeddings(open_jobs)  # Batch of job embeddings

        # Call Triton Inference Server
        client = get_triton_client()
        inputs = [
            grpcclient.InferInput("user_embedding", user_emb.shape, "FP16"),
            grpcclient.InferInput("job_embeddings", job_embs.shape, "FP16"),
        ]
        inputs[0].set_data_from_numpy(user_emb)
        inputs[1].set_data_from_numpy(job_embs)

        outputs = [grpcclient.InferRequestedOutput("similarity_scores")]
        result = client.infer(
            model_name=settings.TRITON_MODEL_NAME,
            inputs=inputs,
            outputs=outputs,
            timeout=settings.TRITON_TIMEOUT_MS / 1000,
        )
        scores = result.as_numpy("similarity_scores")

        # Rank jobs by similarity score
        ranked = sorted(
            zip(open_jobs, scores),
            key=lambda x: x[1],
            reverse=True
        )[:20]  # Top 20 recommendations

        return JsonResponse({
            "user_id": user_id,
            "recommendations": [
                {
                    "job_id": job.id,
                    "title": job.title,
                    "company": job.author.company_name,
                    "score": float(score),
                    "location": job.location.city,
                }
                for job, score in ranked
            ],
            "gpu_info": {
                "available": settings.GPU_AVAILABLE,
                "device": settings.GPU_NAME,
                "inference_ms": result.get_response().request_id,  # trace ID
            },
        })

    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(f"GPU inference failed: {e}", exc_info=True)
        return JsonResponse({"error": "Inference service unavailable"}, status=503)


# Health check endpoint — Prometheus scrapes this
def health_check(request):
    import torch
    return JsonResponse({
        "status": "healthy",
        "gpu": {
            "available": torch.cuda.is_available(),
            "count": torch.cuda.device_count(),
            "name": torch.cuda.get_device_name(0) if torch.cuda.is_available() else None,
            "memory_allocated_mb": torch.cuda.memory_allocated(0) / 1024**2 if torch.cuda.is_available() else 0,
            "memory_reserved_mb": torch.cuda.memory_reserved(0) / 1024**2 if torch.cuda.is_available() else 0,
        },
    })

🚀 CI/CD Pipeline — GitHub Actions for GPU-Accelerated Django

Automate GPU model testing, Docker image building, and deployment with a CI/CD pipeline. GPU runners are expensive — use CPU runners for linting/unit tests, and GPU runners only for model validation.

YAML — .github/workflows/gpu-ci.yml
name: GPU CI/CD Pipeline
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  # Stage 1: Fast linting & unit tests (CPU runner — FREE)
  lint-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: '3.11' }
      - run: pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
      - run: ruff check . && black --check .
      - run: pytest tests/unit/ -v --cov

  # Stage 2: GPU model validation (self-hosted GPU runner)
  gpu-model-test:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, gpu, a100]  # Your DGX or GPU server
    needs: lint-and-test
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Verify GPU available
        run: nvidia-smi && python -c "import torch; assert torch.cuda.device_count() >= 1"
      - name: Load model & run validation
        run: |
          python manage.py warmup_models
          python tests/gpu/test_model_accuracy.py  # Accuracy > 0.85
          python tests/gpu/test_inference_latency.py  # P95 < 50ms
      - name: Export model to TensorRT & validate
        run: |
          python scripts/export_tensorrt.py --model job_pipeline --precision fp16
          python tests/gpu/test_tensorrt_engine.py

  # Stage 3: Build & push Docker image
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: gpu-model-test
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: docker build -t registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-django:${{ github.sha }} .
      - name: Push to registry
        run: |
          docker login registry.anihpj.com -u ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_USER }} -p ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_PASS }}
          docker push registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-django:${{ github.sha }}

  # Stage 4: Deploy to K8s (ArgoCD or kubectl)
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: build-and-push
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    steps:
      - name: Update K8s deployment image
        run: |
          kubectl set image deployment/anihpj-django \
            django=registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-django:${{ github.sha }} \
            -n anihpj-prod
          kubectl rollout status deployment/anihpj-django -n anihpj-prod

🏗️ Infrastructure as Code — Terraform for GPU Clusters

Provision GPU cloud instances declaratively. This Terraform snippet creates an A100 GPU instance on AWS with the NVIDIA GPU Operator pre-configured.

HCL — terraform/gpu-cluster.tf
# ============================================================
# anihpj GPU Infrastructure — AWS p4d.24xlarge (8× A100)
# ============================================================

terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws", version = "~> 5.0" }
    helm = { source = "hashicorp/helm", version = "~> 2.0" }
  }
}

# GPU Instance — p4d.24xlarge = 8× A100 40GB, 96 vCPU, 1.1TB RAM
resource "aws_instance" "gpu_training" {
  ami           = data.aws_ami.nvidia_gpu_ami.id  # NVIDIA GPU-optimized AMI
  instance_type = "p4d.24xlarge"
  count         = var.training_nodes

  # GPU-optimized EBS volumes
  root_block_device {
    volume_type = "gp3"
    volume_size = 200  # GB
    iops        = 16000
    throughput  = 1000  # MB/s
  }

  # NVMe instance store for high-speed scratch
  # 8× 1TB NVMe SSDs included with p4d.24xlarge

  vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.gpu_cluster_sg.id]
  subnet_id              = aws_subnet.gpu_subnet.id

  user_data = templatefile("${path.module}/scripts/gpu_init.sh", {
    cluster_name = var.cluster_name
    nfs_endpoint = aws_efs_file_system.models.dns_name
  })

  tags = {
    Name        = "anihpj-gpu-${count.index}"
    Environment = var.environment
    GPU_Type    = "A100-SXM4-40GB"
    GPU_Count   = "8"
  }
}

# EFS for shared model storage (all GPU nodes access same models)
resource "aws_efs_file_system" "models" {
  performance_mode = "maxIO"  # High throughput for model loading
  throughput_mode  = "bursting"
  tags = { Name = "anihpj-model-registry" }
}

# FSx for Lustre — high-performance parallel storage for training data
resource "aws_fsx_lustre_file_system" "training_data" {
  storage_capacity   = 4800  # 4.8 TB
  deployment_type    = "SCRATCH_2"  # Optimized for throughput
  subnet_ids         = [aws_subnet.gpu_subnet.id]
  security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.gpu_cluster_sg.id]
}

# GPU Node IAM — access to ECR (NGC), S3 (datasets), CloudWatch (logs)
resource "aws_iam_role" "gpu_node" {
  name = "anihpj-gpu-node-role"
  assume_role_policy = jsonencode({
    Version = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = [{
      Effect = "Allow"
      Principal = { Service = "ec2.amazonaws.com" }
      Action = "sts:AssumeRole"
    }]
  })
}

# Output GPU instance IPs for Ansible inventory
output "gpu_ips" {
  value = aws_instance.gpu_training[*].private_ip
}

Appendix E: NVIDIA Glossary — 100+ Terms Defined

📖 A-Z REFERENCE

Every acronym, term, and concept from the NVIDIA ecosystem defined in plain English. This glossary is your quick-reference companion for the NCA-AIIO exam and daily work with NVIDIA infrastructure.

A — Ampere to Attention

Ampere: NVIDIA GPU architecture (2020). A100, 3rd-gen Tensor Cores, TF32, MIG, sparsity. Compute capability 8.0.
Attention Mechanism: The core operation in Transformers. Computes relevance scores between tokens. Computationally expensive — accelerated by Tensor Cores.
Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP): Training technique that uses FP16 for compute and FP32 for accumulation. 2× faster training with minimal accuracy loss.

B — Blackwell to Bus

Blackwell: NVIDIA GPU architecture (2024). B200, 5th-gen Tensor Cores, FP4, 20 PF AI. Named after mathematician David Blackwell.
Base Command Manager (BCM): NVIDIA's cluster management software. Job scheduling, user management, GPU provisioning.
Bandwidth: Data transfer rate. HBM3: 3.35 TB/s. NVLink: 900 GB/s. InfiniBand NDR: 400 GB/s.

C — CUDA to cuQuantum

CUDA: Compute Unified Device Architecture. NVIDIA's parallel computing platform and programming model. Foundation of GPU computing.
CUDA Core: Basic processing unit for integer and FP32/FP64 arithmetic. H100 has 14,592 CUDA Cores.
cuDNN: CUDA Deep Neural Network library. Optimized primitives for convolutions, pooling, normalization.
cuBLAS: CUDA Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms. GPU-accelerated matrix multiplication (GEMM).
cuQuantum: SDK for GPU-accelerated quantum circuit simulation.

D — DCGM to DPU

DCGM: Data Center GPU Manager. Telemetry, health monitoring, diagnostics for NVIDIA GPUs in data centers.
DGX: NVIDIA's purpose-built AI appliance. Pre-configured server with 8 GPUs, NVSwitch, InfiniBand, optimized storage.
DLI: Deep Learning Institute. NVIDIA's training and certification program.
DPU: Data Processing Unit (BlueField). Offloads infrastructure tasks (networking, storage, security) from CPU.

E — ECC to Exclusive Mode

ECC Memory: Error Correcting Code. Detects and corrects memory errors. Essential for HPC and AI training (prevents silent data corruption).
Embarrassingly Parallel: Problem that can be split into many independent tasks. GPUs excel at these. Matrix multiplication is embarrassingly parallel.
Exclusive Mode: GPU compute mode where only one process can use the GPU at a time. Set via nvidia-smi -c 1.

F — FP8 to FLOPS

FP8: 8-bit floating point. Introduced with Hopper (H100). Doubles throughput vs FP16 for AI inference.
FP16: 16-bit half precision. 2× faster than FP32 with minimal accuracy loss. Standard for deep learning training.
FP32: 32-bit single precision. Standard for scientific computing. Higher accuracy than FP16.
FP64: 64-bit double precision. Required for HPC/scientific workloads. A100/H100 have dedicated FP64 Tensor Cores.
FLOPS: Floating Point Operations Per Second. Measure of compute performance. H100: 1,979 TFLOPS FP8.

G — Grace to GPUDirect

Grace CPU: NVIDIA's ARM-based CPU (72 cores, 960 GB/s LPDDR5X bandwidth). Designed for AI workloads.
Grace Hopper Superchip (GH200): Grace CPU + Hopper GPU on one module. NVLink-C2C at 900 GB/s. Coherent memory.
GPU Operator: Kubernetes operator that automates GPU driver, runtime, and monitoring deployment.
GPUDirect: Technology for direct data transfer between GPU memory and third-party devices (NICs, storage) — bypassing CPU memory.

H — HBM to Hyper-Q

HBM: High Bandwidth Memory. Stacked DRAM providing massive bandwidth. HBM3: 3.35 TB/s on H100. HBM3e: 8 TB/s on B200.
HGX: NVIDIA's GPU baseboard. 4-GPU or 8-GPU configurations. Used by OEMs (Dell, HPE) to build AI servers.
Hopper: NVIDIA GPU architecture (2022). H100, 4th-gen Tensor Cores, FP8, Transformer Engine, DPX instructions.
Hyper-Q: Allows multiple CPU threads/processes to launch work on a single GPU simultaneously (32 hardware queues).

I — InfiniBand to INT8

InfiniBand: High-performance interconnect for HPC/AI clusters. NDR400 (400 GB/s), XDR800 (800 GB/s). RDMA support.
INT8: 8-bit integer quantization. 4× faster than FP32 for inference. TensorRT uses INT8 for maximum throughput.
Inference: Using a trained model to make predictions. Typically requires less compute than training. Optimized with TensorRT.

J — Jetson to JIT

Jetson: NVIDIA's edge AI platform. Orin modules for robots, drones, and IoT. Runs CUDA + TensorRT at the edge.
JIT (Just-In-Time): Compilation at runtime. CUDA uses JIT to compile PTX to GPU-specific binary. Numba's @cuda.jit compiles Python to PTX at runtime.

K — Kernel to K8s

Kernel (CUDA): A function that runs on the GPU. Launched with <<<grid, block>>> syntax. Thousands of threads execute the same kernel.
Kubernetes (K8s): Container orchestration. GPU Operator enables GPU scheduling. Resource: nvidia.com/gpu: 1.
KV Cache: Key-Value cache in Transformer inference. Stores attention keys/values to avoid recomputation. Major memory consumer in LLM serving.

L — L40S to LSTM

L40S: Data center GPU based on Ada Lovelace architecture. 48GB GDDR6, 1,466 TFLOPS FP8. Best perf/$ for inference.
Latency: Time to complete one inference request. Critical metric for real-time applications. P95 latency target: <10ms for anihpj.
LLM: Large Language Model. GPT-4, Llama 3, Nemotron. Trained on massive text corpora. Served via Triton + TensorRT-LLM.

M — MIG to Model Parallelism

MIG (Multi-Instance GPU): Partition an A100/H100 into up to 7 independent GPU instances. Each has dedicated memory, cache, and compute.
Mixed Precision: Using FP16 for forward/backward passes and FP32 for weight updates. Standard practice for DL training.
MMLU: Massive Multitask Language Understanding. Standard LLM benchmark covering 57 subjects.
Model Parallelism: Splitting a model across multiple GPUs. Required when model exceeds single GPU memory.

N — NCCL to NVTX

NCCL: NVIDIA Collective Communications Library. Optimized multi-GPU/multi-node communication primitives (all-reduce, all-gather, broadcast).
NGC: NVIDIA GPU Cloud. Container registry and model hub for GPU-optimized software.
NIM: NVIDIA Inference Microservice. Pre-built, optimized containers for deploying AI models.
NVAIE: NVIDIA AI Enterprise. Production-grade AI software suite with enterprise support.
NVTX: NVIDIA Tools Extension. Annotation library for marking code regions in Nsight profiles.

O — Occupancy to OOM

Occupancy: Ratio of active warps to maximum warps per SM. Higher = better latency hiding. Calculated as active_warps / max_warps.
Omniverse: NVIDIA's platform for 3D collaboration and digital twins. Uses USD (Universal Scene Description) format.
ONNX: Open Neural Network Exchange. Interchange format for ML models. Export from PyTorch/TF, deploy on Triton.
OOM (Out of Memory): Fatal GPU error when allocation exceeds available VRAM. Fix: reduce batch size, use gradient checkpointing, or enable MIG.

P — PCIe to PyTorch

PCIe: Peripheral Component Interconnect Express. Connection between CPU and GPU. Gen5: 64 GB/s (x16). NVLink is 14× faster.
Persistence Mode: Keeps NVIDIA driver loaded even when no apps are using GPU. Reduces latency. nvidia-smi -pm 1.
PTX: Parallel Thread Execution. NVIDIA's intermediate assembly language between CUDA C++ and GPU machine code.
PyTorch: Most popular deep learning framework. Native CUDA support. .cuda() moves tensors to GPU.

Q — Quantization to Queue

Quantization: Reducing model precision from FP32 to INT8/FP8/INT4. Reduces memory and increases throughput. TensorRT and bitsandbytes are common tools.
QLoRA: Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation. Fine-tune LLMs on a single GPU by quantizing to 4-bit and adding trainable adapters.
Quantum-2: NVIDIA's 400 GB/s InfiniBand switch platform. 64 ports, 51.2 Tb/s aggregate bandwidth.

R — RAPIDS to RTX

RAPIDS: Suite of GPU-accelerated data science libraries. cuDF (DataFrames), cuML (ML), cuGraph (graph analytics).
RDMA: Remote Direct Memory Access. Network adapter reads/writes GPU memory directly — no CPU involvement.
Register File: Fastest GPU memory. 65,536 × 32-bit registers per SM. More registers/thread = lower occupancy.
RTX: NVIDIA's ray tracing technology. RT Cores accelerate ray-triangle intersections. Omniverse rendering uses RTX.

S — SM to SuperPOD

SM (Streaming Multiprocessor): The building block of NVIDIA GPUs. H100 has 132 SMs. Each SM contains CUDA Cores, Tensor Cores, registers, and shared memory.
Sparsity: Technique to skip zero-valued weights. Ampere+ Tensor Cores support 2:4 structured sparsity for 2× throughput.
SuperPOD: NVIDIA's reference architecture for large-scale AI clusters. 32+ DGX nodes, InfiniBand fabric, validated design.

T — Tensor Core to Triton

Tensor Core: Specialized hardware unit for matrix multiply-accumulate (MMA). The heart of AI acceleration. 4th Gen on H100 supports FP8, FP16, TF32, FP64.
TensorRT: NVIDIA's inference optimization SDK. Layer fusion, kernel auto-tuning, precision calibration (FP32→FP16→INT8).
TF32: TensorFloat-32. 19-bit format using FP32 range + FP16 precision. 8× faster than FP32 on A100 with no code changes.
Triton: NVIDIA's multi-framework inference server. Supports PyTorch, TF, ONNX, TensorRT, custom backends. Dynamic batching.

U-V — USD to VRAM

USD (Universal Scene Description): Pixar's 3D interchange format. Omniverse uses USD as its native format.
vGPU: Virtual GPU. Shares a physical GPU across multiple VMs. Used for VDI, cloud gaming, and multi-tenant AI.
VRAM: Video RAM. GPU's onboard memory. H100: 80 GB HBM3. Consumer GPUs use GDDR6/GDDR6X. Critical for model size.

W-Z — Warp to Zero-Copy

Warp: Group of 32 threads that execute in lockstep on an SM. Fundamental unit of GPU execution. Divergence within a warp serializes execution.
XID Error: NVIDIA GPU fatal hardware error. XID 48 = double-bit ECC. XID 74 = NVLink error. XID 79 = GPU fell off bus. GPU replacement indicator.
Zero-Copy: Technique where GPU directly accesses host (CPU) memory over PCIe/NVLink. Avoids explicit cudaMemcpy. Lower bandwidth than device memory.

📝 NCA-AIIO Exam: 15 Must-Know Terms

These terms appear in 80%+ of NCA-AIIO exam questions. Master them first: CUDA (parallel computing platform), Tensor Core (MMA hardware unit), NVLink (GPU-to-GPU interconnect at 900 GB/s), MIG (GPU partitioning for multi-tenancy), HBM (high-bandwidth GPU memory), SM (Streaming Multiprocessor — the GPU building block), Occupancy (active warps / max warps), NCCL (multi-GPU communication), TensorRT (inference optimizer), FP8 (Hopper's 8-bit AI precision), InfiniBand (cluster interconnect), DCGM (GPU telemetry), Triton (inference server), DGX (AI appliance), and Grace Hopper (CPU+GPU superchip).

🛠️ Practical Terms Every GPU SRE Uses Daily

Beyond the formal glossary, these are the terms you'll hear in GPU infrastructure meetings, Slack channels, and incident calls:

GPU Lingo in Production

GPU Hung: GPU stopped responding. Usually requires reset (nvidia-smi -r) or power cycle.
GPU Starvation: GPU is idle because CPU can't feed data fast enough. Fix: increase batch size, use async data loader.
GPU Fragmentation: Multiple small jobs leave GPU memory fragments — can't fit a large job even though total free memory is sufficient. MIG helps.
Thermal Throttling: GPU automatically reduces clock speed to prevent overheating. Indicates cooling failure.
ECC Storm: Sudden spike in ECC error corrections. Often precedes a memory bank failure. Watch for XID 48.

MLOps & Infra Slang

Cold Start: First inference after model loads — slow because GPU memory is cold. Warm-up requests fix this.
GPU Bin Packing: Fitting multiple workloads onto one GPU to maximize utilization. MIG or MPS (Multi-Process Service).
Model Bloat: Model grew too large for GPU memory after fine-tuning. Fix: quantization, pruning, or bigger GPU.
GPU Fleece: Cloud provider charges for GPU but delivers degraded performance (throttled, shared, or older-gen). Verify with nvidia-smi.
N+1 GPU Redundancy: Keep one spare GPU per cluster for failover — not capacity. Hot spare vs cold spare.

Performance Terminology

Roofline Model: Visual tool showing if your kernel is compute-bound or memory-bound. The "roof" is peak FLOPS and peak memory BW.
Arithmetic Intensity: FLOPS / bytes accessed. High AI = compute-bound (Tensor Cores help). Low AI = memory-bound (need better caching).
Tail Latency: P99/P99.9 latency. The slowest 1% of requests. GPU inference tail latency often caused by batch padding or CPU-GPU sync.
GPU-Day: One GPU running for 24 hours. Standard unit for measuring AI compute cost. "That experiment cost 80 GPU-days on A100."

Infrastructure Acronyms

BOM: Bill of Materials — complete parts list for a GPU server/cluster.
MTBF: Mean Time Between Failures. GPU MTBF ~3-5 years. NVSwitch MTBF ~5-7 years.
TOPS/W: TOPS per Watt. Energy efficiency metric. H100: ~3 TOPS/W (1,979 TOPS / 700W).
GPU TCO: Total Cost of Ownership. Hardware + power + cooling + maintenance + support over 3-5 years.
SLA: Service Level Agreement. NVAIE includes 24/7 support SLA. Open-source = no SLA (you're on your own at 2 AM).

📋 NCA-AIIO Exam Day Checklist

✅ Before the Exam

• Schedule exam 2-4 weeks out for focused prep time
• Review all 300 questions in this guide — know the explanations
• Take 3 timed mock exams (90 min each) — aim for 80%+
• Memorize: GPU specs table, NVCC -arch flags, DCGM commands
• Test your Pearson VUE system 48 hours before
• Prepare ID (must match registration name exactly)

❌ During the Exam — Avoid

• Don't spend > 2 min on any question — flag and return
• Don't second-guess your first answer unless certain
• Don't leave any question unanswered (no penalty for guessing)
• Don't get stuck on performance-based questions
• Don't use external resources (proctored — no notes)

🧪 Hands-On Practice

NVIDIA DLI: Free GPU cloud labs for courses.
Google Colab: Free T4 GPU (limited). Good for learning.
Lambda Labs: Rent A100/H100 by the hour.
vast.ai: Peer-to-peer GPU rental. Cheapest for practice.

🏆 Exam Time Strategy

• 0-10 min: Skim all. Answer easy ones (~30%)
• 10-60 min: Work medium. Flag hard (~50%)
• 60-80 min: Return to flagged. Eliminate wrong options.
• 80-90 min: Review all. Verify no blanks. Submit.

🆓 How to Get Free GPU Credits

• Google Cloud: $300 free credit for new accounts (90 days). Enough for ~200 hrs of A100.
• AWS Activate: Up to $100K in credits for startups. Includes GPU instances.
• Azure for Startups: Up to $150K in credits. Includes ND A100 v4 instances.
• NVIDIA Inception: Free for AI startups. Cloud credits, hardware discounts, technical support.
• Academic Programs: NSF ACCESS (US researchers), XSEDE — free GPU hours for research.

📋 Registration Process

1. Create account at nvidia.com/certification
2. Select exam → Pearson VUE checkout
3. Choose: Online proctored (OnVUE) or Test center
4. Online: Test your system 48 hrs before. Need webcam, quiet room, no dual monitors.
5. Test center: Arrive 30 min early with 2 forms of ID.
6. Results: Immediately after exam (provisional pass/fail).
7. Badge: Credly digital badge within 48 hrs of passing.

🏆 Final Words — The Journey Continues

You've completed 30 chapters, 300 practice questions, and 6 comprehensive appendices. You understand GPU architecture from the transistor level to the data center scale. You can write CUDA kernels, deploy models on Triton, design GPU clusters, and monitor infrastructure with DCGM.

But more importantly, you understand why accelerated computing matters. It's not just about faster computation — it's about solving problems that were previously impossible. Drug discovery, climate modeling, autonomous vehicles, and generative AI all depend on the technology you now understand deeply.

"Accelerated computing is the path forward. The more you buy, the more you save." — Jensen Huang

Now go build something that matters. The GPU clusters are waiting. 🚀
